lessons.title: A function that remembers its own data
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 1: A function that remembers its own data

theory.contentHtml:
So far you have written functions to take something in and give something back. But an R function also keeps hold of what it could see when it was born - and that is the tidiest way to produce a family of nearly identical functions without copying code.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Functions that make functions
  2. Where the remembered value lives
  3. A counter with its own state
  4. The lazy evaluation trap
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. Functions that make functions

A function can return another function:

make_tax <- function(rate) {
  function(amount) amount * rate
}

vat <- make_tax(0.1)
luxury <- make_tax(0.35)

cat("VAT:", vat(1000), "\n")
cat("Luxury tax:", luxury(1000), "\n")

Output:

VAT: 100
Luxury tax: 350

vat and luxury are two different functions from the same mould, differing in exactly one thing - the rate each one keeps for itself.

Without this you would either write two nearly identical functions, or pass rate on every call, when rate is precisely the thing that never changes.

2. Where the remembered value lives

What the inner function remembers is called its environment. You can look at it:

make_tax <- function(rate) {
  function(amount) amount * rate
}

vat <- make_tax(0.1)

print(ls(environment(vat)))
print(get("rate", environment(vat)))

Output:

[1] "rate"
[1] 0.1

rate is not a global variable, and it is not a parameter of vat. It lives in the environment attached to vat, and it survives for as long as vat does.

A function carrying its environment like this is called a closure.

3. A counter with its own state

Because that environment persists, a function can change what it remembers. The <<- operator assigns to a variable in the enclosing environment instead of creating a new one inside:

make_counter <- function() {
  n <- 0
  function() {
    n <<- n + 1
    n
  }
}

hits <- make_counter()
cat(hits(), hits(), hits(), "\n")

other <- make_counter()
cat("an independent counter:", other(), "\n")

Output:

1 2 3
an independent counter: 1

other starts again at 1 - each call to make_counter() creates its own environment. This is how R keeps state without a global variable, which anything else in the program could overwrite.

4. The lazy evaluation trap

R does not evaluate an argument until it actually needs it. Inside a loop, that bites:

makers <- list()
for (i in 1:3) {
  local({
    j <- i
    makers[[j]] <<- function() j
  })
}

cat(makers[[1]](), makers[[2]](), makers[[3]](), "\n")

Output:

1 2 3

Here local() together with j <- i makes a private copy for each pass, so the three functions return 1, 2 and 3 as expected.

Drop the local() and all three look at one variable i, which is 3 by the time the loop ends - so all three return 3. The more reliable fix is to force evaluation immediately:

make_adder <- function(n) {
  force(n)
  function(x) x + n
}

add5 <- make_adder(5)
cat(add5(10), "\n")

Output:

15

Function reference

+----------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
|    Function    |                                   What it does                                   |            Example            |
+----------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
| environment(f) | Returns the environment a function carries with it                               | environment(vat)              |
| ls(env)        | Lists the names bound in an environment                                          | ls(environment(vat))          |
| get(name, env) | Reads one binding out of a given environment                                     | get("rate", environment(vat)) |
| <<-            | Assigns to a variable in the enclosing environment instead of creating a new one | n <<- n + 1                   |
| local(expr)    | Runs an expression in its own throwaway environment                              | local({ j <- i; ... })        |
| force(x)       | Evaluates an argument now instead of leaving it lazy                             | force(n)                      |
+----------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+

Key takeaways

A closure is a function plus a memory. Same mould, different remembered value. When you catch yourself about to write two functions that differ only by a constant, that is the signal to reach for one.

<<- changes a variable in the enclosing environment, <- creates a new one inside. Confusing the two leaves your counter forever returning 1, with nothing in the code looking wrong.

R evaluates arguments lazily. Making functions in a loop without force() is the classic failure: every function produced ends up bound to the loop variable's final value.

lessons.title: Folding a whole sequence into one result
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 2: Folding a whole sequence into one result

theory.contentHtml:
You have used sapply to apply a function to each element. But some jobs are not "do this to each one" - they are "fold them all into one", or "keep only the ones that qualify". R has a function for each shape, and each reads out its intent far faster than a loop does.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Folding a sequence into one value
  2. Keeping the elements that qualify
  3. Joining many tables into one
  4. Passing a function as an argument
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. Folding a sequence into one value

Reduce() takes the first two elements, applies the function, then combines that result with the third, and so on:

nums <- c(4, 7, 2, 9)

cat("sum:", Reduce(`+`, nums), "\n")
cat("largest:", Reduce(function(a, b) if (a > b) a else b, nums), "\n")

Output:

sum: 22
largest: 9

For addition, sum() already exists. Reduce earns its keep when the combining step has no ready-made function - for instance the intersection of several sets:

groups <- list(
  c("an", "binh", "chi", "dung"),
  c("binh", "chi", "dung", "em"),
  c("chi", "dung", "phuc")
)

print(Reduce(intersect, groups))

Output:

[1] "chi"  "dung"

Three lists, and you want whoever appears in all three. No function takes a list and does that directly - Reduce runs intersect down the chain.

Add accumulate = TRUE to see every step, which is exactly what a running total needs:

revenue <- c(120, 85, 200, 60)
print(Reduce(`+`, revenue, accumulate = TRUE))

Output:

[1] 120 205 405 465

Each number is the running total at that point - 120, then 120+85, then plus 200, finally plus 60.

2. Keeping the elements that qualify

Filter() states the intent "keep only the ones where…" directly:

salaries <- list(an = 12, binh = 25, chi = 18, dung = 31)

high <- Filter(function(x) x > 20, salaries)
print(names(high))

Output:

[1] "binh" "dung"

For a vector, salaries[salaries > 20] is shorter. Filter comes into its own on a list, where subsetting with brackets gets awkward.

Map() applies a function across several sequences in parallel:

price <- c(20, 15, 30)
qty <- c(3, 10, 2)

totals <- Map(function(p, q) p * q, price, qty)
print(unlist(totals))

Output:

[1]  60 150  60

3. Joining many tables into one

This is where Reduce shows up most in real work - several tables to join on the same key:

q1 <- data.frame(region = c("North", "South"), q1 = c(120, 200))
q2 <- data.frame(region = c("North", "South"), q2 = c(150, 260))
q3 <- data.frame(region = c("North", "South"), q3 = c(180, 240))

report <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "region"), list(q1, q2, q3))
print(report)

Output:

region  q1  q2  q3
1  North 120 150 180
2  South 200 260 240

With three tables, writing merge twice by hand is fine. With twelve monthly tables, Reduce is the difference between one line and a screenful.

4. Passing a function as an argument

Because a function in R is an ordinary value, you pass it around like a number:

summarise_by <- function(values, f) f(values)

x <- c(3, 9, 4, 12)
cat(summarise_by(x, mean), summarise_by(x, max), summarise_by(x, sd), "\n")

Output:

7 12 4.242641

That is exactly what makes sapply, Reduce and Filter possible: they are simply functions that take another function.

Function reference

+---------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
|             Function            |                               What it does                              |                 Example                 |
+---------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| Reduce(f, x)                    | Folds a sequence into one value, combining pairwise from the left       | Reduce(intersect, groups)               |
| Reduce(f, x, accumulate = TRUE) | Same, but keeps every step - what a running total needs                 | Reduce(sum, revenue, accumulate = TRUE) |
| Filter(f, x)                    | Keeps only the elements for which f returns TRUE                        | Filter(function(x) x > 20, salaries)    |
| Map(f, x, y)                    | Applies a function across several sequences in parallel, returns a list | Map(function(p, q) p * q, price, qty)   |
| unlist(x)                       | Flattens a list into a vector                                           | unlist(totals)                          |
| intersect(a, b)                 | Elements present in both vectors                                        | intersect(g1, g2)                       |
| merge(a, b, by =)               | Joins two tables on a shared key column                                 | merge(q1, q2, by = "region")            |
+---------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

Pick the function that matches the shape of the job. Do it to each one → sapply/lapply. Fold into one → Reduce. Keep some → Filter. Several sequences in step → Map. Naming the job correctly means whoever reads the code sees the intent immediately.

Reduce is not faster than a loop. What it buys you is legible intent. For speed, look for an already-vectorised function (sum, cumsum, pmax) - see the performance module.

Backticks around an operator. \+`` is how you refer to addition as a function. It looks odd, but that is simply its name.

lessons.title: Calling a function when the arguments are not known yet
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 3: Calling a function when the arguments are not known yet

theory.contentHtml:
Sometimes you only learn at run time how many arguments a call will have, or you want a function that accepts extra options and passes them straight down to another one. R has three tools for exactly that, and knowing them removes a lot of long if chains.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Calling with a list of arguments
  2. Receiving and forwarding options
  3. Restricting what callers may pass
  4. Stacking tables of the same shape
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. Calling with a list of arguments

do.call() takes a function and a list of arguments, then calls it as if you had typed them:

args <- list(1:10)
cat(do.call(mean, args), "\n")

args2 <- list(c(3, NA, 5), na.rm = TRUE)
cat(do.call(mean, args2), "\n")

Output:

5.5
4

The key point: the argument list is now data. You build it with code, according to the situation, and only then make the call.

build_args <- function(drop_na) {
  a <- list(c(10, NA, 20, 30))
  if (drop_na) a$na.rm <- TRUE
  a
}

cat("keeping NA:", do.call(mean, build_args(FALSE)), "\n")
cat("dropping NA:", do.call(mean, build_args(TRUE)), "\n")

Output:

keeping NA: NA
dropping NA: 20

The same mean, differing only in whether the argument list carries na.rm - and code decides that at run time.

2. Receiving and forwarding options

The dots ... collect every remaining argument and pass them on untouched:

describe <- function(x, ...) {
  cat("mean:", mean(x, ...), "\n")
  cat("standard deviation:", sd(x, ...), "\n")
}

describe(c(4, NA, 8, 10), na.rm = TRUE)

Output:

mean: 7.333333
standard deviation: 3.05505

You never have to re-declare na.rm, trim and every other option mean supports. Whoever calls describe gets all of them.

To see what ... is holding, turn it into a list:

show_extra <- function(x, ...) {
  extra <- list(...)
  cat("extra arguments:", length(extra), "\n")
  print(names(extra))
}

show_extra(1:5, na.rm = TRUE, trim = 0.1)

Output:

extra arguments: 2
[1] "na.rm" "trim"

3. Restricting what callers may pass

When a parameter accepts only a few values, match.arg() sets the default, gives a clear error on anything else, and allows abbreviations:

summarise_as <- function(x, how = c("mean", "median", "max")) {
  how <- match.arg(how)
  switch(how, mean = mean(x), median = median(x), max = max(x))
}

x <- c(5, 1, 9, 3)
cat(summarise_as(x), summarise_as(x, "median"), summarise_as(x, "max"), "\n")

Output:

4.5 4 9

The first value in the vector is the default. Passing "medi" still works because match.arg matches on prefix; passing "average" fails immediately with the list of valid values - instead of quietly falling into the wrong branch.

4. Stacking tables of the same shape

This is the most common use of do.call:

months <- list(
  data.frame(region = "North", revenue = 120),
  data.frame(region = "South", revenue = 200),
  data.frame(region = "Central", revenue = 90)
)

all <- do.call(rbind, months)
print(all)

Output:

region revenue
1   North     120
2   South     200
3 Central      90

rbind wants the tables as separate arguments, and what you have is one list. do.call is the bridge: it spreads the list out into individual arguments.

Function reference

+----------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
|          Function          |                             What it does                             |            Example            |
+----------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
| do.call(f, args)           | Calls f with an argument list built beforehand                       | do.call(mean, list(1:10))     |
| ...                        | Collects the remaining arguments and forwards them untouched         | function(x, ...) mean(x, ...) |
| list(...)                  | Turns the dots into a list so you can inspect or count them          | extra <- list(...)            |
| names(x)                   | Element names - with list(...) it tells you what the caller passed   | names(extra)                  |
| match.arg(arg)             | Sets the default, matches on prefix, errors clearly on anything else | how <- match.arg(how)         |
| switch(x, a = , b = )      | Picks a branch by string, shorter than a chain of if                 | switch(how, mean = mean(x))   |
| do.call(rbind, list_of_df) | Stacks a list of same-shaped tables into one table                   | do.call(rbind, months)        |
+----------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+

Key takeaways

do.call(f, list(...)) calls f with an argument list you assembled first. Use it when the number or names of arguments are only known at run time.

... forwards options down to the function underneath. It makes your function flexible without restating every argument of the original.

match.arg turns a silent failure into a loud one. Without it, a mistyped string falls through to switch's default branch and produces a wrong number nobody notices.

lessons.title: Quiz Functions as values
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 4: Quiz Functions as values

questions.prompt: make_tax <- function(rate) function(amount) amount * rate. After vat <- make_tax(0.1), where does rate live?

options.label: A
options.text: In the global environment

options.label: B
options.text: In the environment attached to vat, for as long as vat exists

options.label: C
options.text: It is deleted as soon as make_tax returns

options.label: D
options.text: It becomes a second parameter of vat

questions.explanation: The inner function carries the environment it was born in - that is a closure. rate is not global: typing rate at the console reports it as not found. Nor is it cleaned up when make_tax returns, because the inner function still references that environment, so the garbage collector leaves it alone. You can see it directly with ls(environment(vat)) and get("rate", environment(vat)). This is exactly why vat and luxury, from the same mould, give different answers.

questions.prompt: In make_counter, what happens if you replace n <<- n + 1 with n <- n + 1?

options.label: A
options.text: No difference

options.label: B
options.text: The counter increases by 2 each time

options.label: C
options.text: R reports a syntax error

options.label: D
options.text: The counter always returns 1, because each call creates a new local n

questions.explanation: <- creates a variable inside the function; <<- assigns to the one in the enclosing environment. With n <- n + 1, R still finds the old n (which is 0) by lexical scope in order to compute, but the resulting 1 is bound to a new local `n` that disappears when the function returns - so the next call starts from 0 again. No error, no warning, just a counter stuck at 1. This class of bug is hard to spot because the code looks entirely reasonable.

questions.prompt: You have 12 monthly revenue tables in a list and need to join them all on region. What is the tidiest way?

options.label: A
options.text: Write 11 merge calls in sequence

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "region"), tables)

options.label: C
options.text: sapply(tables, merge)

options.label: D
options.text: Filter(merge, tables)

questions.explanation: Reduce runs a two-argument combining step down the whole sequence: it merges table 1 with table 2, merges that result with table 3, and so on to the end. sapply applies a function to each element separately, so there is nowhere for the result to accumulate - it hands back twelve things rather than one. Filter only keeps the elements that qualify; it combines nothing. Writing 11 merge calls by hand does work, but it is long, and one more month means editing the code.

questions.prompt: You have a list of data frames with the same shape and want to stack them. Why does rbind(tables) not do what you want?

options.label: A
options.text: Because rbind wants the tables as separate arguments and you are handing it one list - you need do.call(rbind, tables)

options.label: B
options.text: Because rbind only accepts matrices

options.label: C
options.text: Because the tables must have the same number of rows

options.label: D
options.text: Because they need sorting first

questions.explanation: rbind(tables) hands rbind exactly one argument - the whole list - so there is nothing to stack against anything. do.call(rbind, tables) spreads the list out into separate arguments, precisely as if you had typed rbind(tables[[1]], tables[[2]], ...) yourself. That is the bridge between "my data is a list" and "this function takes many arguments", and it is the most common use of do.call in real work.

questions.prompt: summarise_as <- function(x, how = c("mean", "median", "max")) with how <- match.arg(how). What happens on summarise_as(x, "average")?

options.label: A
options.text: It runs and returns the mean

options.label: B
options.text: It fails immediately, listing the valid values

options.label: C
options.text: It returns NULL

options.label: D
options.text: It silently falls back to mean

questions.explanation: That is the reason to use match.arg: a mistyped string becomes a loud failure at the point of the mistake, complete with the list of valid values so the caller can fix it. Without it, switch("average", mean = ..., median = ..., max = ...) matches no branch and returns NULL with no warning - the function still runs, and the result still travels on into the report. Note that match.arg also matches on prefix, so "medi" is perfectly valid.

questions.prompt: What is the classic bug when you create functions in a loop without force() or local()?

options.label: A
options.text: The loop runs more slowly

options.label: B
options.text: Only the first function works

options.label: C
options.text: Every function produced ends up bound to the final value of the loop variable

options.label: D
options.text: R runs out of memory

questions.explanation: R evaluates arguments lazily - nothing is computed until it is needed. All the functions produced in the loop look at one loop variable rather than private copies, and by the time they are actually called the loop finished long ago and that variable holds its final value. The result: three functions you believed were different return the same number. Fix it with force() to evaluate immediately, or local() to give each pass its own copy.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?


revenue <- c(120, 85, 200, 60)
print(Reduce(`+`, revenue, accumulate = TRUE))
questions.explanation: accumulate = TRUE keeps every step rather than only the final result, so the output is exactly as long as the input: 120, then 120+85=205, then +200=405, then +60=465. Drop accumulate and you get the single number 465 (answer a). This is how you compute a running total without writing a loop - the same idea as cumsum() for addition, except Reduce works with any two-argument combining step.

lessons.title: Drawing a line through a cloud of points
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 5: Drawing a line through a cloud of points

theory.contentHtml:
You have used plot() to see that ad spend and revenue move together. The next question anyone doing this for real asks is: how closely, and how much more revenue does one more million of spend buy. That is what linear regression answers, and in R it is surprisingly short.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. One line to fit a model
  2. The two numbers that matter most
  3. Seeing that line on the chart
  4. Adding a second explanatory variable
  5. Reading the whole summary() table
  6. Function reference
  7. Key takeaways

1. One line to fit a model

The ~ reads as "by": revenue ~ ad_spend means revenue by ad spend.

sales <- data.frame(
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40),
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310)
)

model <- lm(revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales)
print(coef(model))

Output:

(Intercept)    ad_spend
  39.285714    6.571429

Those two numbers are the model:

  • (Intercept) - estimated revenue when ad spend is zero
  • ad_spend - the extra revenue for each additional unit of spend

The second number is the one you can take into a meeting. It answers exactly the question "spend one more, get how much more".

2. The two numbers that matter most

summary() prints a long table. Early on, two places are enough:

sales <- data.frame(
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40),
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310)
)

s <- summary(lm(revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales))

cat("slope:", round(coef(s)[2, 1], 2), "\n")
cat("p-value:", format.pval(coef(s)[2, 4], digits = 3), "\n")
cat("R squared:", round(s$r.squared, 3), "\n")

Output:

slope: 6.57
p-value: 2.23e-06
R squared: 0.992
  • The coefficient's p-value: small (0.05 is the usual mark) means this relationship is unlikely to be luck alone.
  • R squared: the share of variation in revenue the model accounts for, between 0 and 1. It is near 1 here because the sample data is unrealistically tidy - real numbers rarely are.

3. Seeing that line on the chart

The numbers tell half the story, the picture tells the other half:

library(ggplot2)

sales <- data.frame(
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40),
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310)
)

ggplot(sales, aes(x = ad_spend, y = revenue)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1e40af") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#2563eb") +
  labs(title = "Revenue by ad spend", x = "Ad spend", y = "Revenue")

geom_smooth(method = "lm") draws exactly the line lm() just found. Always look before trusting the numbers: if the points bend into a clear U, a straight line is the wrong description no matter how high R squared is.

4. Adding a second explanatory variable

Revenue rarely depends on one thing. A + adds another variable:

shops <- data.frame(
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310),
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40),
  staff = c(2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5)
)

model <- lm(revenue ~ ad_spend + staff, data = shops)
print(round(coef(model), 2))

Output:

(Intercept)    ad_spend       staff
      24.88        4.74       18.33

The ad_spend coefficient now reads: extra revenue per unit of ad spend, holding staff constant. That "holding the other thing constant" clause is the biggest difference between multiple and simple regression.

5. Reading the whole summary() table

Section 2 pulled out three numbers. But summary() prints a whole table, and sooner or later you will meet it intact in somebody else's report:

sales <- data.frame(
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40),
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310)
)

print(summary(lm(revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales)))

Output:

Call:
lm(formula = revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales)

Residuals:
         1          2          3          4          5          6          7
 3.331e-14  2.143e+00  4.286e+00 -8.571e+00  3.571e+00 -9.286e+00  7.857e+00

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  39.2857     7.2983   5.383  0.00298 **
ad_spend      6.5714     0.2711  24.244 2.23e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Residual standard error: 7.171 on 5 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9916,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.9899
F-statistic: 587.8 on 1 and 5 DF,  p-value: 2.225e-06

Reading down the table:

  • Residuals - the residuals themselves. The sample here is small, so R prints all seven; from 8 rows up (once the residual degrees of freedom pass 5) it switches to the five-number Min/1Q/Median/3Q/Max summary. Either way, what matters is whether the residuals lean heavily to one side - a lean is a sign the model has the wrong shape.
  • Estimate - the coefficients. This column answers the business question.
  • Std. Error - the uncertainty in each coefficient. A slope of 6.57 with a standard error of 0.25 is one thing; the same 6.57 with a standard error of 6 is another entirely.
  • t value = Estimate divided by Std. Error. The larger it is, the more the coefficient stands out from the noise.
  • Pr(>|t|) - the p-value for that coefficient alone. The stars beside it are just a quick marker for the familiar thresholds.
  • Residual standard error - an estimate of the standard deviation of the in-sample residuals, in the response's units. It describes spread around the fitted line; it is not a guaranteed prediction error for a new observation (a prediction interval is wider because it includes additional uncertainty).
  • Multiple R-squared and Adjusted - the adjusted version penalises adding variables. Add a useless variable and plain R squared usually still creeps up, while the adjusted one falls.
  • F-statistic with the p-value at the end - a test of the whole model, not of any single coefficient. With one predictor it coincides with that predictor's p-value.

Do not read this table top to bottom out of habit. The order worth reading is: the coefficient first (it answers the question), then its standard error, then the residual standard error, and only then R squared.

Function reference

+----------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
|          Function          |                                      What it does                                     |                 Example                |
+----------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| lm(y ~ x, data =)          | Fits a linear model; ~ reads as "by"                                                  | lm(revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales)   |
| lm(y ~ x1 + x2)            | Adds explanatory variables with +                                                     | lm(revenue ~ ad_spend + staff)         |
| coef(model)                | The coefficient vector on its own                                                     | coef(model)                            |
| summary(model)             | The full table: coefficients, errors, p-values, R squared                             | summary(model)                         |
| s$r.squared                | Pulls R squared out of a summary()                                                    | summary(model)$r.squared               |
| coef(s)                    | The coefficient matrix of a summary(); column 1 is the estimate, column 4 the p-value | coef(s)[2, 4]                          |
| format.pval(p)             | Prints a very small p-value compactly instead of 0.00000                              | format.pval(p, digits = 3)             |
| geom_smooth(method = "lm") | Draws exactly the line lm() found                                                     | geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) |
+----------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

The slope is the answer for the meeting. "One more million of ad spend is associated with about X million more revenue" is a sentence people understand - R squared is not.

A high R squared does not mean the model is right. It only says the model fits the data you already have. A straight line can fit curved data closely.

Moving together is not causing. Regression measures association, it does not establish cause. Claims about cause need an experiment, not another variable in the model.

lessons.title: The part the model gets wrong
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 6: The part the model gets wrong

theory.contentHtml:
Every model gets things wrong. That wrongness is where you find out whether the model is usable - and it says more than any summary statistic.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. What a residual is
  2. Predicting for new data
  3. Reading residuals by eye
  4. When one point drags the whole line
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. What a residual is

Residual = actual − predicted. Positive means the model came in low, negative means it came in high.

sales <- data.frame(
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40),
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310)
)

model <- lm(revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales)

out <- data.frame(
  actual = sales$revenue,
  predicted = round(fitted(model), 1),
  residual = round(resid(model), 1)
)
print(out)

Output:

actual predicted residual
1    105     105.0      0.0
2    140     137.9      2.1
3    175     170.7      4.3
4    195     203.6     -8.6
5    240     236.4      3.6
6    260     269.3     -9.3
7    310     302.1      7.9

The residuals always sum to roughly zero - that is how lm picks the line. So do not look at the total, look at the shape.

2. Predicting for new data

predict() applies the model to data it has never seen:

sales <- data.frame(
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40),
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310)
)
model <- lm(revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales)

new_plan <- data.frame(ad_spend = c(22, 45))
print(round(predict(model, newdata = new_plan), 1))

Output:

1     2
183.9 335.0

Note the spend of 45: it is outside the range the model learned from (10–40). The model cheerfully returns a number anyway, but nothing guarantees the linear relationship still holds out there. This is the most common trap when models are used for planning.

To get an interval with it:

sales <- data.frame(
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40),
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310)
)
model <- lm(revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales)

print(round(predict(model, data.frame(ad_spend = 22), interval = "confidence"), 1))

Output:

fit   lwr   upr
1 183.9 176.6 191.1

fit is the prediction, lwr/upr are the two ends of the confidence interval. Reporting the interval is always more honest than reporting a bare number.

3. Reading residuals by eye

Residuals plotted against fitted values should look like a shapeless cloud. A shape means the model is missing something:

library(ggplot2)

curved <- data.frame(x = 1:12)
curved$y <- (curved$x - 6)^2 + 10

model <- lm(y ~ x, data = curved)

ggplot(data.frame(predicted = fitted(model), residual = resid(model)),
       aes(x = predicted, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#2563eb") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "A clear U in the residuals means the relationship is not linear",
       x = "Predicted value", y = "Residual")

An unmistakable U: the data curves, and we forced a straight line through it. R squared will not say this - only the picture will.

4. When one point drags the whole line

A single unusual observation can bend the model on its own:

base <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), y = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10))
with_outlier <- rbind(base, data.frame(x = 20, y = 5))

cat("without outlier, slope:", round(coef(lm(y ~ x, base))[2], 2), "\n")
cat("with outlier,    slope:", round(coef(lm(y ~ x, with_outlier))[2], 2), "\n")

Output:

without outlier, slope: 2
with outlier,    slope: 0.02

One row pulls the slope from 2 down to near 0. That is why you plot the data before modelling it - and why "remove the outlier" is never a purely technical decision: you have to ask why that point exists.

Function reference

+---------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
|                Function               |                             What it does                             |                   Example                   |
+---------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| fitted(model)                         | What the model predicts for the data it learned from                 | fitted(model)                               |
| resid(model)                          | Residuals = actual − predicted                                       | resid(model)                                |
| predict(model, newdata =)             | Applies the model to new data                                        | predict(model, newdata = new_plan)          |
| predict(..., interval = "confidence") | Adds an interval: columns fit, lwr, upr                              | predict(model, df, interval = "confidence") |
| geom_hline(yintercept =)              | Draws a horizontal reference line - fits the zero line for residuals | geom_hline(yintercept = 0)                  |
| rbind(a, b)                           | Appends rows to a table                                              | rbind(base, data.frame(x = 20, y = 5))      |
+---------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

Shape in the residuals means the wrong model shape. A formless cloud is good; a U, a funnel, or a drift are all signs of a missing variable or the wrong functional form.

Predicting outside the learned range is decorated guessing. The model does not know it has left safe ground, and it will not warn you.

One unusual point can steer the whole model. Plot first, model second. And when you find an outlier, the first question is whether it is a data-entry error or a real event.

lessons.title: Putting a categorical variable into the model
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 7: Putting a categorical variable into the model

theory.contentHtml:
Real data is rarely all numbers. Region, channel, plan - those are factors, and the way R handles them in a regression is worth understanding properly, because otherwise you will read the output table wrongly.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. One categorical variable in the model
  2. What the reference group is
  3. Changing the reference group
  4. Mixing numeric and categorical
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. One categorical variable in the model

staff <- data.frame(
  salary = c(12, 14, 13, 22, 25, 24, 17, 18, 19),
  team = factor(c("Sales", "Sales", "Sales", "Tech", "Tech", "Tech", "HR", "HR", "HR"))
)

model <- lm(salary ~ team, data = staff)
print(round(coef(model), 2))

Output:

(Intercept)   teamSales    teamTech
      18.00       -5.00        5.67

Three groups, but only two coefficients. Not a bug - that is how R encodes a factor.

2. What the reference group is

For a character vector freshly converted with factor(x), R sorts levels alphabetically by default. Under the default treatment contrasts, the current first level is the reference - here HR. An existing factor may carry a different level order, and contrasts can be configured differently, so inspect levels() instead of guessing. The baseline has no separate coefficient because it is absorbed into (Intercept):

staff <- data.frame(
  salary = c(12, 14, 13, 22, 25, 24, 17, 18, 19),
  team = factor(c("Sales", "Sales", "Sales", "Tech", "Tech", "Tech", "HR", "HR", "HR"))
)
model <- lm(salary ~ team, data = staff)

cat("levels:", levels(staff$team), "\n")
cat("HR mean:", mean(staff$salary[staff$team == "HR"]), "\n")
cat("(Intercept):", round(coef(model)[1], 2), "\n")
cat("teamTech   :", round(coef(model)["teamTech"], 2), "\n")
cat("Tech mean  :", mean(staff$salary[staff$team == "Tech"]), "\n")

Output:

levels: HR Sales Tech
HR mean: 18
(Intercept): 18
teamTech   : 5.67
Tech mean  : 23.66667

Read it like this: (Intercept) is the mean of the reference group; teamTech is the difference from the reference group, not Tech's value. Add the two to get Tech's mean.

This is the single most common misreading of a regression table containing factors.

3. Changing the reference group

The reference should be the group that is meaningful to compare against, not whichever comes first alphabetically:

staff <- data.frame(
  salary = c(12, 14, 13, 22, 25, 24, 17, 18, 19),
  team = factor(c("Sales", "Sales", "Sales", "Tech", "Tech", "Tech", "HR", "HR", "HR"))
)

staff$team <- relevel(staff$team, ref = "Sales")
print(round(coef(lm(salary ~ team, data = staff)), 2))

Output:

(Intercept)      teamHR    teamTech
      13.00        5.00       10.67

Now every coefficient reads "how much more than Sales" - sensible when Sales is the company's baseline.

4. Mixing numeric and categorical

shops <- data.frame(
  revenue = c(105, 140, 175, 195, 240, 260, 310, 150),
  ad_spend = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 18),
  channel = factor(c("Online", "Store", "Online", "Store", "Online", "Store", "Online", "Store"))
)

model <- lm(revenue ~ ad_spend + channel, data = shops)
print(round(coef(model), 2))

Output:

(Intercept)     ad_spend channelStore
       42.80         6.59        -9.72

The channelStore coefficient reads: the revenue difference between Store and Online, at the same ad spend. That last clause is what simply comparing two group means cannot give you.

Function reference

+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
|         Function        |                                    What it does                                   |               Example              |
+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
| factor(x)               | Marks a column as categorical rather than a measurement                           | factor(c("Sales", "Tech"))         |
| levels(f)               | The groups in the order R is using - the first is the reference                   | levels(staff$team)                 |
| relevel(f, ref =)       | Moves the reference to a group that makes business sense                          | relevel(staff$team, ref = "Sales") |
| lm(y ~ f)               | Regression on a factor; each coefficient is a difference from the reference group | lm(salary ~ team, data = staff)    |
| coef(model)["teamTech"] | Pulls one coefficient out by name                                                 | coef(model)["teamTech"]            |
| round(x, 2)             | Rounds so the coefficient table stays readable                                    | round(coef(model), 2)              |
+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

A factor coefficient is a DIFFERENCE, not a value. teamTech = 5 means Tech sits 5 units above the reference group. Reading it as "Tech's salary is 5" is completely wrong.

Under the default treatment contrasts, the reference is the current first level. factor(character_vector) usually creates alphabetical levels, but an existing factor may have another order. Inspect levels() and use relevel() to choose a meaningful baseline.

Remember factor() for categorical variables. If groups are coded as numbers (1, 2, 3) and you forget to convert, R treats them as a continuous quantity and the model becomes meaningless.

lessons.title: Quiz Linear regression
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 8: Quiz Linear regression

questions.prompt: lm(revenue ~ ad_spend, data = sales) gives an ad_spend coefficient of 6.8. How do you read that?

options.label: A
options.text: Average revenue is 6.8

options.label: B
options.text: One more unit of ad spend is associated with about 6.8 more units of revenue

options.label: C
options.text: The model explains 6.8% of the variation

options.label: D
options.text: There is a 6.8% chance the relationship is random

questions.explanation: The slope is the change in the outcome per unit change in the explanatory variable - exactly the "spend one more, get how much more" a meeting is asking for. The three wrong answers are three other numbers from the same table that people routinely confuse it with: share of variation explained is R squared, the chance the relationship is luck alone is the p-value, and the mean of the outcome is not printed here at all. Mistaking the slope for one of those is the most common early error when reading a regression table.

questions.prompt: A model has R squared = 0.95. Which conclusion is CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: The model definitely has the right shape

options.label: B
options.text: It fits the data you have well, but may still be the wrong shape - check the residuals

options.label: C
options.text: Ad spend causes revenue

options.label: D
options.text: Predictions at any spend level are trustworthy

questions.explanation: R squared only measures fit on the data the model learned from; it says nothing about whether the shape is right. A straight line can reach 0.95 on data that genuinely curves - and only the residual plot reveals the U. It says nothing about causation either (regression measures association, it does not establish a cause), and it certainly does not make predictions outside the learned range trustworthy. Adding any variable almost always nudges R squared up, even a meaningless one - which is why summary also prints the adjusted version.

questions.prompt: Residuals plotted against fitted values form a clear U. What does that tell you?

options.label: A
options.text: The data has many outliers

options.label: B
options.text: The sample is too small

options.label: C
options.text: The real relationship is not linear - forcing a straight line is the wrong shape

options.label: D
options.text: The model fits perfectly

questions.explanation: Residuals plotted against fitted values should look like a shapeless cloud. A shape means the model is missing structure that is still sitting in the data - here, the curvature. Outliers show up as a few isolated points far from the rest, not as the whole cloud bending into a U. A small sample makes residuals sparse and harder to read, but it does not manufacture a shape. The fix is to change the model's shape (add a quadratic term, take logs) or add the missing variable - not to delete points until the picture looks nicer.

questions.prompt: The model learned on spend of 10–40. You call predict() for 45. What happens?

options.label: A
options.text: R errors because it is out of range

options.label: B
options.text: R returns an ordinary number, but nothing guarantees the relationship still holds there

options.label: C
options.text: R clips it back to 40

options.label: D
options.text: The result is always NA

questions.explanation: The model does not know it has left the data it learned from, and it has no mechanism to warn you: predict simply substitutes into the equation of the line. The number that comes back looks exactly like an ordinary prediction, even when the spend is far beyond anything ever observed. The real risk is that a linear relationship usually only holds over a range - outside it things can saturate or reverse. The safe practice is to report the interval alongside it and to state whether the prediction sits inside or outside the observed range.

questions.prompt: lm(salary ~ team) with three groups HR/Sales/Tech prints only two coefficients. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: One group has missing data

options.label: B
options.text: It needs a manual factor() call

options.label: C
options.text: R caps factors at two coefficients

options.label: D
options.text: One group is the reference and is absorbed into (Intercept)

questions.explanation: Under the default treatment contrasts, R uses the current first level as the baseline and absorbs it into (Intercept). Here factor() created alphabetical levels, so that is HR, but an existing factor may have a different order - inspect levels(). The remaining coefficients are differences from the baseline; k groups give k−1 coefficients. Use relevel() to change it.

questions.prompt: In lm(salary ~ team) with HR as baseline, teamTech = 8 and (Intercept) = 18. What is Tech's mean salary?

options.label: D
options.text: Not enough information

questions.explanation: A factor coefficient is a difference from the reference, so Tech's mean = (Intercept) + teamTech = 18 + 8 = 26. Reading it as "Tech earns 8" (answer a) is the most common error with factor regression tables; and 18 is the mean of the baseline group HR, not Tech. The information is sufficient - that is precisely what makes this encoding compact: each group costs one number, and that number always reads as "how much more than the baseline".

questions.prompt:
In the summary() of a one-predictor model you see:


Residual standard error: 7.171 on 5 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9916,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.9899


What does 7.171 tell you?

options.label: A
options.text: The estimated standard deviation of the in-sample residuals, in units of revenue

options.label: B
options.text: The percentage of variation the model fails to explain

options.label: C
options.text: The standard error of the slope

options.label: D
options.text: The number of observations dropped from the model

questions.explanation: Residual standard error estimates the standard deviation of residuals around the fitted line and carries the response's units. It is neither mean absolute error nor a guaranteed error for a new observation; prediction intervals include additional uncertainty. Unexplained variation is read from R squared, while the slope's uncertainty is its Std. Error.

chapters.title: A REAL DIFFERENCE OR JUST LUCK

lessons.title: Are these two groups genuinely different
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 9: Are these two groups genuinely different

theory.contentHtml:
Group A averages 24, group B averages 26. Should you say "B is better than A"? The answer depends on how much each group varies inside itself and on the sample size - two things that comparing two averages never mentions.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Why comparing averages is not enough
  2. A t-test for two groups
  3. Reading a p-value correctly
  4. The confidence interval says more
  5. Four wrong things people say about p-values
  6. Function reference
  7. Key takeaways

1. Why comparing averages is not enough

Two datasets with the same gap between the means, and completely different conclusions:

tight_a <- c(24, 24, 25, 23, 24)
tight_b <- c(26, 26, 25, 27, 26)

noisy_a <- c(5, 40, 12, 38, 25)
noisy_b <- c(30, 8, 45, 15, 32)

cat("tight:", mean(tight_a), "vs", mean(tight_b), "\n")
cat("noisy:", mean(noisy_a), "vs", mean(noisy_b), "\n")
cat("tight sd:", round(sd(tight_a), 1), round(sd(tight_b), 1), "\n")
cat("noisy sd:", round(sd(noisy_a), 1), round(sd(noisy_b), 1), "\n")

Output:

tight: 24 vs 26
noisy: 24 vs 26
tight sd: 0.7 0.7
noisy sd: 15.5 14.6

The same gap of 2. But in the first set every value clusters tightly, so a gap of 2 stands out; in the second the data swings from 5 to 45, so a gap of 2 says nothing at all.

2. A t-test for two groups

t.test() works that out for you:

tight_a <- c(24, 24, 25, 23, 24)
tight_b <- c(26, 26, 25, 27, 26)

result <- t.test(tight_a, tight_b)
cat("difference in means:", round(diff(rev(result$estimate)), 2), "\n")
cat("p-value:", format.pval(result$p.value, digits = 3), "\n")

Output:

difference in means: -2
p-value: 0.00208

And on the noisy pair:

noisy_a <- c(5, 40, 12, 38, 25)
noisy_b <- c(30, 8, 45, 15, 32)

cat("p-value:", format.pval(t.test(noisy_a, noisy_b)$p.value, digits = 3), "\n")

Output:

p-value: 0.839

The same difference, two opposite conclusions - matching the intuition from section 1, now as a number.

3. Reading a p-value correctly

A p-value answers one narrow question: if the two groups really were no different, how likely is a gap at least as large as the one observed?

set.seed(42)
same_a <- rnorm(30, mean = 50, sd = 10)
same_b <- rnorm(30, mean = 50, sd = 10)

cat("two groups drawn from the SAME distribution\n")
cat("p-value:", round(t.test(same_a, same_b)$p.value, 3), "\n")

Output:

two groups drawn from the SAME distribution
p-value: 0.526

These two groups come from exactly the same distribution - no difference whatsoever - and the p-value is still not 1. Randomness always produces some gap.

Three things a p-value does not tell you:

  • It is not "the probability the groups are the same".
  • It says nothing about how large the difference is.
  • It says nothing about whether the difference matters to the business.

With a very large sample, a difference of 0.1% that is meaningless in practice still produces a tiny p-value.

4. The confidence interval says more

tight_a <- c(24, 24, 25, 23, 24)
tight_b <- c(26, 26, 25, 27, 26)

ci <- t.test(tight_a, tight_b)$conf.int
cat("95% confidence interval for the difference:", round(ci[1], 2), "to", round(ci[2], 2), "\n")

Output:

95% confidence interval for the difference: -3.03 to -0.97

This gives the size of the difference, not just whether there is one. If the interval contains zero, the difference is not clear-cut; if it sits entirely in a range too small to care about, you know immediately there is nothing to act on.

5. Four wrong things people say about p-values

All four sentences below turn up regularly in presentations, and all four are wrong.

"p = 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the groups are the same." The p-value is computed assuming the groups are the same - it is not the probability of that assumption. Getting a probability of that kind requires a different approach (Bayesian) and information beyond the data.

"p = 0.06 means there is no difference." Failing to reject is not proof of equality. A small sample gives a large p even when a real difference exists - exactly the "noisy" pair from section 1: p = 0.839 while the difference in means is still 2.

"A tiny p means a big difference." This is the one that costs money. With a large enough sample, a difference nobody cares about still produces a minuscule p:

set.seed(7)
big_a <- rnorm(200000, mean = 100.0, sd = 15)
big_b <- rnorm(200000, mean = 100.2, sd = 15)

cat("observed difference:", round(mean(big_b) - mean(big_a), 3), "\n")
cat("p-value:", format.pval(t.test(big_a, big_b)$p.value, digits = 3), "\n")

Output:

observed difference: 0.208
p-value: 1.18e-05

The difference is far too small to change anything, yet the p-value looks "significant". That is why the confidence interval from section 4 matters more than the p itself: it tells you how much, not just whether.

"p = 0.049 is meaningfully different from p = 0.051." The 0.05 mark is a human convention, not a boundary in nature. Those two results are all but identical; report the p alongside the confidence interval instead of sorting results into "significant" and "not".

Function reference

+--------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
|      Function      |                            What it does                            |            Example            |
+--------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
| t.test(x, y)       | Compares two group means, accounting for spread and sample size    | t.test(tight_a, tight_b)      |
| $p.value           | Pulls the p-value out of a test result                             | t.test(a, b)$p.value          |
| $conf.int          | Confidence interval for the difference - the thing worth reporting | t.test(a, b)$conf.int         |
| $estimate          | The mean of each group                                             | t.test(a, b)$estimate         |
| sd(x)              | Standard deviation - how much the group varies internally          | sd(tight_a)                   |
| format.pval(p)     | Prints a very small p-value compactly                              | format.pval(p, digits = 3)    |
| set.seed(n)        | Fixes the random generator so results reproduce                    | set.seed(42)                  |
| rnorm(n, mean, sd) | Draws n random values from a normal distribution                   | rnorm(30, mean = 50, sd = 10) |
+--------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+

Key takeaways

A gap between means only means something alongside the spread. The same distance can be decisive or meaningless, depending on whether the data clusters or scatters.

A small p means "unlikely if there were no difference", not "a large difference". The 0.05 mark is a convention, not a boundary of truth.

Always report the confidence interval. It answers what your audience actually wants to know: different by how much.

lessons.title: Are two characteristics related
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 10: Are two characteristics related

theory.contentHtml:
The previous lesson was about numbers. When both quantities are categories - purchase channel and whether the customer came back - the tools are quite different: a cross-tabulation and a chi-squared test.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. A two-way table
  2. The chi-squared test
  3. What you would expect if there were no link
  4. When the counts are small
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. A two-way table

table() takes two vectors and counts the pairs:

channel <- c(rep("Online", 60), rep("Store", 40))
returned <- c(rep("Yes", 18), rep("No", 42), rep("Yes", 20), rep("No", 20))

tab <- table(channel, returned)
print(tab)
print(round(prop.table(tab, margin = 1), 2))

Output:

returned
channel  No Yes
  Online 42  18
  Store  20  20
        returned
channel   No Yes
  Online 0.7 0.3
  Store  0.5 0.5

prop.table(tab, margin = 1) divides by row, giving the rate within each channel - the only numbers that compare, because the two channels have different totals.

Online 30% returned, Store 50%. The gap looks clear, but the question remains: could it be luck?

2. The chi-squared test

channel <- c(rep("Online", 60), rep("Store", 40))
returned <- c(rep("Yes", 18), rep("No", 42), rep("Yes", 20), rep("No", 20))
tab <- table(channel, returned)

result <- chisq.test(tab)
cat("X-squared:", round(result$statistic, 3), "\n")
cat("p-value:", format.pval(result$p.value, digits = 3), "\n")

Output:

X-squared: 3.27
p-value: 0.0706

Note that p = 0.0706 is not below the familiar 0.05 mark, even though 30% against 50% looked so clear in section 1. A sample of 100 is not enough to rule out luck - a good reminder not to read 0.05 as a yes/no boundary.

The hypothesis under test is "the two characteristics are independent". A small p means the data is unlikely if they were independent - evidence of a link.

3. What you would expect if there were no link

This is what makes the test intelligible, rather than a p-value you take on faith:

channel <- c(rep("Online", 60), rep("Store", 40))
returned <- c(rep("Yes", 18), rep("No", 42), rep("Yes", 20), rep("No", 20))
tab <- table(channel, returned)

cat("observed:\n")
print(tab)
cat("\nexpected if independent:\n")
print(round(chisq.test(tab)$expected, 1))

Output:

observed:
        returned
channel  No Yes
  Online 42  18
  Store  20  20

expected if independent:
        returned
channel    No  Yes
  Online 37.2 22.8
  Store  24.8 15.2

The "expected" table is the counts you would see if the return rate were the same in both channels. The test only measures the distance between those two tables. The further apart, the larger the statistic and the smaller the p.

4. When the counts are small

Chi-squared is an approximation, and it stops being trustworthy when cells hold very few observations:

small <- matrix(c(2, 3, 4, 1), nrow = 2,
                dimnames = list(channel = c("Online", "Store"), returned = c("Yes", "No")))
print(small)

cat("\nFisher p-value:", round(fisher.test(small)$p.value, 3), "\n")

Output:

returned
channel  Yes No
  Online   2  4
  Store    3  1

Fisher p-value: 0.524

For a 2×2 table with small counts, fisher.test() is the right choice - it computes exactly rather than approximating. Running chisq.test here makes R warn you, and that warning deserves to be heard.

Function reference

+-----------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------+
|           Function          |                               What it does                              |             Example             |
+-----------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------+
| table(x, y)                 | Counts the pairs, giving a two-way table                                | table(channel, returned)        |
| prop.table(tab, margin = 1) | Turns counts into rates by row - the comparable numbers                 | prop.table(tab, margin = 1)     |
| chisq.test(tab)             | Tests whether two characteristics are independent                       | chisq.test(tab)                 |
| $expected                   | The counts expected under independence - what the test compares against | chisq.test(tab)$expected        |
| $statistic                  | The X-squared value, measuring observed-versus-expected distance        | chisq.test(tab)$statistic       |
| fisher.test(tab)            | Exact test for a 2×2 table with small counts                            | fisher.test(small)              |
| rep(x, n)                   | Repeats a value n times - handy for building sample data                | rep("Online", 60)               |
| matrix(..., dimnames =)     | Builds a table directly, with row and column names                      | matrix(c(2, 3, 4, 1), nrow = 2) |
+-----------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------+

Key takeaways

Compare rates, not raw counts. When groups have different totals, the counts say nothing - prop.table(tab, margin = 1) gives the comparable numbers.

Chi-squared says "there is a link", not "which one causes which". Nor does it say how strong the link is.

Small counts call for fisher.test. The chisq.test warning about an unreliable approximation is a real warning, not noise.

lessons.title: Comparing more than two groups
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 11: Comparing more than two groups

theory.contentHtml:
You have four groups and want to know whether they differ. The instinctive move is to run t.test on every pair. That is the trap, and this lesson explains why, along with the right approach.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Why testing every pair is wrong
  2. One test for all the groups
  3. Which group differs from which
  4. Look before you test
  5. Assumptions and effect size
  6. Function reference
  7. Key takeaways

1. Why testing every pair is wrong

Each test at the 0.05 level carries a 5% false-alarm rate when its null is true. If the tests are independent, the illustrative formula 1 - (1 - alpha)^m shows how the chance of at least one false alarm climbs fast:

for (k in c(2, 4, 6, 10)) {
  pairs <- choose(k, 2)
  risk <- 1 - 0.95^pairs
  cat(k, "groups ->", pairs, "pairs ->", round(risk * 100, 1), "% chance of a false alarm\n")
}

Output:

2 groups -> 1 pairs -> 5 % chance of a false alarm
4 groups -> 6 pairs -> 26.5 % chance of a false alarm
6 groups -> 15 pairs -> 53.7 % chance of a false alarm
10 groups -> 45 pairs -> 90.1 % chance of a false alarm

Six groups make 15 pairs; in the independent-test illustration the risk exceeds 50%. Pairwise tests on the same data are actually dependent, so 53.7% is not their exact probability - but family-wise error is still inflated and must be controlled. Bonferroni gives the upper bound min(1, m * alpha); ANOVA followed by Tukey HSD is a better workflow when comparing every pair.

2. One test for all the groups

Analysis of variance asks a single question: "is any group different from the rest?"

scores <- data.frame(
  value = c(72, 75, 71, 74, 80, 82, 79, 81, 68, 66, 70, 67),
  branch = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 4))
)

fit <- aov(value ~ branch, data = scores)
print(summary(fit))

Output:

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)
branch       2  328.5  164.25   62.24 5.37e-06 ***
Residuals    9   23.8    2.64
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

The Pr(>F) column is the p-value. Small means at least one group stands apart - but it does not say which.

3. Which group differs from which

Once the overall test shows a signal, then you look at pairs, with an adjustment for having looked many times:

scores <- data.frame(
  value = c(72, 75, 71, 74, 80, 82, 79, 81, 68, 66, 70, 67),
  branch = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 4))
)

print(TukeyHSD(aov(value ~ branch, data = scores)))

Output:

Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = value ~ branch, data = scores)

$branch
      diff        lwr       upr     p adj
B-A   7.50   4.292905 10.707095 0.0002837
C-A  -5.25  -8.457095 -2.042905 0.0034529
C-B -12.75 -15.957095 -9.542905 0.0000040

Each row is one pair: the difference, a confidence interval, and an adjusted p. Any pair whose interval spans zero is not a clear difference.

Alternatively, use t-tests directly but adjust the p-values:

scores <- data.frame(
  value = c(72, 75, 71, 74, 80, 82, 79, 81, 68, 66, 70, 67),
  branch = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 4))
)

print(pairwise.t.test(scores$value, scores$branch, p.adjust.method = "holm"))

Output:

Pairwise comparisons using t tests with pooled SD

data:  scores$value and scores$branch

  A       B
B 0.00022 -
C 0.00135 4.5e-06

P value adjustment method: holm

Read the table by row and column: the B–A cell is the p-value for the B-versus-A pair. All three pairs come out small, agreeing with Tukey above - two different adjustments, the same answer.

4. Look before you test

library(ggplot2)

scores <- data.frame(
  value = c(72, 75, 71, 74, 80, 82, 79, 81, 68, 66, 70, 67),
  branch = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 4))
)

ggplot(scores, aes(x = branch, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#bfdbfe") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, size = 2, color = "#1e40af") +
  labs(title = "Scores by branch", x = NULL, y = "Score")

The boxes show range and median, the dots show every actual observation. If the picture already makes clear that B sits above C, the test merely confirms it; if the groups overlap almost completely, treat any small p-value with suspicion.

5. Assumptions and effect size

One-way ANOVA assumes independent observations, approximately normal residuals within groups, and sufficiently similar variances. Independence comes from the data-collection design; no diagnostic plot can establish it. Paired, repeated-measure, or branch-clustered data need another model. Use residual and Q-Q plots to diagnose shape and variance; with strongly unequal variances consider Welch ANOVA, while ordinal data or severe outliers may call for robust/non-parametric methods.

A p-value does not say how large a difference is. Report Tukey differences and confidence intervals, plus an overall effect size such as eta squared = SS_between / SS_total. Interpret effect size in the business context rather than applying one mechanical threshold across every field.

Function reference

+------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
|                 Function                 |                               What it does                               |                     Example                     |
+------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| aov(y ~ f, data =)                       | Analysis of variance - one test across all groups                        | aov(value ~ branch, data = scores)              |
| summary(fit)                             | The ANOVA table; Pr(>F) is the overall p-value                           | summary(fit)                                    |
| TukeyHSD(fit)                            | Pairwise comparisons after ANOVA, adjusted for multiple looks            | TukeyHSD(aov(...))                              |
| pairwise.t.test(x, g, p.adjust.method =) | The same job with a choice of adjustment method                          | pairwise.t.test(v, g, p.adjust.method = "holm") |
| choose(k, 2)                             | Number of pairs from k groups - the number of tests you are about to run | choose(6, 2)                                    |
| geom_boxplot()                           | Box: median and spread for each group                                    | geom_boxplot(fill = "#bfdbfe")                  |
| geom_jitter(width =)                     | Nudges each point so you see the real data, not only the summary         | geom_jitter(width = 0.08)                       |
+------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

Testing many pairs inflates the false-alarm rate. 1-(1-alpha)^m is exact only for independent tests; pairs sharing groups are not independent. The valid conclusion is still that family-wise error needs control.

Right order: overall test → if there is a signal → adjusted pairwise comparisons. Jumping straight to pairwise tests manufactures findings.

Plot first, test second. A test gives you a number; the picture tells you whether to trust it.

Check design and assumptions, then report effect size. A small p cannot rescue dependent data or a misspecified model, and it does not say whether the difference matters in practice.
