lessons.title: Quiz A real difference or just luck
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 12: Quiz A real difference or just luck

questions.prompt: Two datasets both show a gap of exactly 2 between the group means, but one has a standard deviation of 0.8 and the other 16. What follows?

options.label: A
options.text: Both give the same conclusion, since the gap is the same

options.label: B
options.text: In the low-spread set the gap is clear-cut; in the high-spread set a gap of 2 says nothing

options.label: C
options.text: The high-spread set is more reliable because it holds more information

options.label: D
options.text: You cannot compare them without equal sample sizes

questions.explanation: A gap between means only means something read alongside the spread within each group. That is exactly what t.test weighs up for you.

questions.prompt: p-value = 0.03. Which reading is CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: If the groups really were no different, a gap at least this large would occur 3% of the time

options.label: B
options.text: There is a 3% chance the two groups are the same

options.label: C
options.text: The difference between the groups is 3%

options.label: D
options.text: The model explains 97% of the variation

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of the data under the assumption of no difference, not the probability of that assumption. It also says nothing about the size of the difference.

questions.prompt: Very large sample, p-value < 0.001, actual difference 0.1%. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Roll it out - the result is statistically significant

options.label: B
options.text: Look at the confidence interval and ask whether 0.1% matters to the business

options.label: C
options.text: Drop some data so the p-value rises

options.label: D
options.text: Conclude the groups are identical

questions.explanation: With a large enough sample, any tiny difference produces a small p. Statistical significance and practical significance are different things.

questions.prompt: Cross-tab: Online 18 of 60 returned, Store 20 of 40. Why not compare 18 with 20 directly?

options.label: A
options.text: Because raw counts are always wrong

options.label: B
options.text: Because the table needs sorting first

options.label: C
options.text: Because the channels have different totals - compare 30% with 50%

options.label: D
options.text: Because table() miscounts

questions.explanation: prop.table(tab, margin = 1) divides by row to give the rate within each group - the only comparable number when the groups differ in size.

questions.prompt: You have 6 groups and plan to run unadjusted t.test on all 15 pairs at the 0.05 level. What is the risk?

options.label: A
options.text: It takes a long time to run

options.label: B
options.text: Family-wise error is inflated; its exact level depends on dependence among tests

options.label: C
options.text: No risk if the data is clean

options.label: D
options.text: Every p-value comes out as 1

questions.explanation: Many unadjusted tests increase the probability of at least one false alarm. 1 − 0.95¹⁵ exceeds 50% only in the illustrative independent-test model; pairs sharing groups are dependent, so that is not their exact probability. Use ANOVA with adjusted post-hoc comparisons, or another appropriate family-wise-error control.

questions.prompt: aov() returns a very small Pr(>F). What can you conclude at that point?

options.label: A
options.text: Group A differs from group B

options.label: B
options.text: The groups are the same

options.label: C
options.text: All three groups differ from each other

options.label: D
options.text: At least one group stands apart from the rest, but not yet which one

questions.explanation: The overall test only answers yes or no for the whole set. Finding out which pair takes TukeyHSD or an adjusted pairwise.t.test. Going straight to the pairs and skipping the overall test walks back into the multiple-comparison trap from the start of the lesson. ANOVA also says nothing about how large any difference is - for that, read Tukey's diff column together with its confidence interval.

questions.prompt:
A cross-tab of 100 orders shows 30% returns online and 50% in store. The test gives:


X-squared: 3.27
p-value: 0.0706


What is the correct conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: It is proven that both channels have the same return rate

options.label: B
options.text: The observed gap is 20 percentage points, but 100 orders is not enough to rule out luck

options.label: C
options.text: There is a 7.06% chance the two channels are the same

options.label: D
options.text: The test misfired, since p should be small for a gap that large

questions.explanation: This is the most commonly misread case: the gap looks obvious yet p stays above 0.05. Sample size drives certainty, and 100 orders split across four cells is not much. Failing to reject is not proof of equality (answer a) - it only means this data cannot settle the question. Nor is p the probability that the channels are the same (answer c): it is computed assuming they are. The right move is to collect more data, not to try tests until one gives a pleasing number.

chapters.title: CHARTS THAT SAY WHAT YOU MEAN

lessons.title: Adjusting axes and colour scales
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 13: Adjusting axes and colour scales

theory.contentHtml:
ggplot2's defaults are good, but a default does not know what story you are telling. The three things you adjust most are the axis, the colour scale and number formatting - and each one changes how the picture is understood.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Formatting numbers on an axis
  2. Choosing the axis range
  3. Colour scales on your terms
  4. Flipping when labels are long
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. Formatting numbers on an axis

An axis showing 3e+05 is an unfinished chart. The labels argument of scale_y_continuous() takes a function:

library(ggplot2)

sales <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "Central"),
  revenue = c(320000, 480000, 210000)
)

ggplot(sales, aes(x = region, y = revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x / 1000, "k")) +
  labs(title = "Revenue by region", x = NULL, y = "Thousands")

That function receives the axis values and returns the labels - so you can format however you like: percentages, currency, thousands or millions.

2. Choosing the axis range

coord_cartesian() zooms without discarding data:

library(ggplot2)

trend <- data.frame(month = 1:12, rate = c(94, 95, 94, 96, 95, 97, 96, 97, 96, 98, 97, 98))

ggplot(trend, aes(x = month, y = rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2563eb", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(90, 100)) +
  labs(title = "On-time delivery rate", x = "Month", y = "%")

The important distinction: coord_cartesian(ylim = ...) only changes the view, while scale_y_continuous(limits = ...) removes points outside the range before drawing - so it can distort a mean or a trend line without saying a word.

3. Colour scales on your terms

When colour carries business meaning, do not leave the choice to the library:

library(ggplot2)

status <- data.frame(
  month = rep(c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar"), each = 2),
  outcome = rep(c("On time", "Late"), 3),
  orders = c(120, 12, 140, 8, 155, 20)
)

ggplot(status, aes(x = month, y = orders, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("On time" = "#16a34a", "Late" = "#dc2626")) +
  labs(title = "Delivery outcome by month", x = NULL, y = "Orders", fill = NULL)

Green for on time, red for late - the reader understands before reaching the legend. For a continuous scale use scale_fill_gradient(low = , high = ).

4. Flipping when labels are long

library(ggplot2)

products <- data.frame(
  name = c("Wireless mechanical keyboard", "Premium optical mouse", "27-inch curved monitor",
           "Noise-cancelling headphones", "High-resolution webcam"),
  revenue = c(120, 240, 310, 180, 90)
)

ggplot(products, aes(x = reorder(name, revenue), y = revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Revenue by product", x = NULL, y = "Millions")

coord_flip() swaps the axes so long labels sit horizontally and stay readable instead of colliding or being tilted. Pair it with reorder() so the bars are ordered - people read a list top to bottom.

Function reference

+------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------+
|              Function              |                          What it does                         |                         Example                        |
+------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------+
| scale_y_continuous(labels =)       | Reformats axis labels; takes a function from number to string | labels = function(x) paste0(x / 1000, "k")             |
| coord_cartesian(ylim =)            | Zooms the view, keeping all data and every computed statistic | coord_cartesian(ylim = c(90, 100))                     |
| scale_y_continuous(limits =)       | Sets a range but drops points outside it before drawing       | scale_y_continuous(limits = c(90, 100))                |
| scale_fill_manual(values =)        | Assigns fixed colours to named groups                         | values = c("Pass" = "#16a34a")                         |
| scale_fill_gradient(low =, high =) | A continuous colour scale for a numeric quantity              | scale_fill_gradient(low = "#eff6ff", high = "#1e40af") |
| coord_flip()                       | Swaps the axes so long labels stay readable                   | coord_flip()                                           |
| reorder(x, y)                      | Orders groups by value instead of alphabetically              | reorder(name, revenue)                                 |
| labs(fill = NULL)                  | Drops the legend title when the colours already speak         | labs(fill = NULL)                                      |
+------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

coord_cartesian zooms, scale_*_continuous(limits=) cuts. Confuse them and your trend line is computed on a silently trimmed dataset.

Meaningful colour must be set by hand. Pass/fail, profit/loss, safe/risky - letting the library pick at random makes the reader consult a legend for something that should be obvious.

For long labels, flip the axis rather than tilting the text. Text at 45 degrees is markedly harder to read than horizontal text.

lessons.title: Putting the note on the chart itself
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 14: Putting the note on the chart itself

theory.contentHtml:
A good chart states its own conclusion instead of asking the reader to work it out. The way to do that is to put text and reference marks directly on the picture, rather than leaving everything to the commentary.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Numbers on top of the bars
  2. A reference line to compare against
  3. Pointing at the thing worth noticing
  4. Titles that state the finding
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. Numbers on top of the bars

geom_text() is a drawing layer like any other:

library(ggplot2)

sales <- data.frame(region = c("North", "South", "Central"), revenue = c(320, 480, 210))

ggplot(sales, aes(x = region, y = revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  geom_text(aes(label = revenue), vjust = -0.4, size = 4) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 560)) +
  labs(title = "Revenue by region", x = NULL, y = NULL)

vjust = -0.4 lifts the text above the bar. Raise the ceiling a little, or the label on the tallest bar gets clipped.

Once the numbers sit on the bars, the y axis is redundant - drop it and the chart gets cleaner.

2. A reference line to compare against

A number only means something next to a benchmark:

library(ggplot2)

trend <- data.frame(month = 1:8, rate = c(88, 91, 87, 93, 95, 92, 96, 97))
target <- 95

ggplot(trend, aes(x = month, y = rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2563eb", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = target, linetype = "dashed", color = "#dc2626") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = target + 1.2, label = "Target 95%", color = "#dc2626") +
  labs(title = "On-time rate by month", x = "Month", y = "%")

annotate() differs from geom_text() in that it draws one thing at fixed coordinates rather than reading from the data. Using geom_text here would stack the same sentence on itself, once per row of data.

3. Pointing at the thing worth noticing

library(ggplot2)

trend <- data.frame(month = 1:8, revenue = c(120, 130, 128, 135, 210, 140, 138, 145))

ggplot(trend, aes(x = month, y = revenue)) +
  geom_line(color = "#94a3b8") +
  geom_point(color = "#94a3b8") +
  geom_point(data = subset(trend, revenue > 200), color = "#dc2626", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 225, label = "Promotion campaign", color = "#dc2626") +
  labs(title = "Revenue by month", x = "Month", y = "Millions")

Fade the background and highlight the point you are talking about. This is the single most effective technique in the lesson: instead of asking the reader to search, you point.

4. Titles that state the finding

library(ggplot2)

channel <- data.frame(channel = c("Online", "Store"), rate = c(30, 50))

ggplot(channel, aes(x = channel, y = rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = c("#94a3b8", "#dc2626")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(rate, "%")), vjust = -0.4, size = 5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "In-store returns run at nearly double the online rate",
    subtitle = "Q3 2026 · 100 orders",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  )

Compare: "Return rate by channel" only says what the chart is about. "In-store returns run at nearly double the online rate" states the finding. Someone skimming reads only the title - let the title do the work.

Function reference

+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
|               Function              |                            What it does                            |                      Example                      |
+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| geom_text(aes(label =))             | Draws text from the data - one label per row                       | geom_text(aes(label = revenue), vjust = -0.4)     |
| annotate("text", x =, y =, label =) | Draws one item at a fixed coordinate, independent of the data      | annotate("text", x = 2, y = 96, label = "Target") |
| vjust / hjust                       | Nudges text up/down, left/right from its anchor                    | vjust = -0.4                                      |
| geom_hline(yintercept =)            | A horizontal reference line - target, threshold, average           | geom_hline(yintercept = 95, linetype = "dashed")  |
| geom_vline(xintercept =)            | A vertical reference line, often marking a point in time           | geom_vline(xintercept = 5)                        |
| geom_point(data = subset(...))      | Overlays a second point layer for just the part being highlighted  | geom_point(data = subset(trend, revenue > 200))   |
| labs(subtitle =)                    | The line under the title - where the data range and sample size go | labs(subtitle = "Q3 2026 · 100 orders")           |
| coord_cartesian(ylim =)             | Raises the ceiling so labels on the tallest bar are not clipped    | coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 560))                 |
+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

annotate() for fixed text, geom_text() for data-driven text. Get it backwards and the same sentence is drawn hundreds of times, blurring the chart for no visible reason.

Raise the axis ceiling when labelling bars. Otherwise the label on the tallest bar is cut off.

The title is where the conclusion belongs. It is the one line certain to be read.

lessons.title: How charts lie
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 15: How charts lie

theory.contentHtml:
The same numbers, two ways of drawing them, two opposite conclusions - without changing a single figure. Learn these tricks so you never use them by accident, and so you spot them when someone else does.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Cutting off the axis
  2. Choosing a flattering time window
  3. Raw counts instead of rates
  4. Pie charts and what the eye cannot measure
  5. Checking your own chart
  6. Function reference
  7. Key takeaways

1. Cutting off the axis

library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(group = c("A", "B"), score = c(96, 98))

ggplot(d, aes(x = group, y = score)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(95, 99)) +
  labs(title = "B massively outperforms A (?)", x = NULL, y = "Score")

Bar B looks several times taller than bar A. Now draw it from zero:

library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(group = c("A", "B"), score = c(96, 98))

ggplot(d, aes(x = group, y = score)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "The real gap: 2 points on a scale of 100", x = NULL, y = "Score")

Two points out of a hundred. With bars, height is the message, so cutting the baseline distorts it directly. With a trend line, zooming is reasonable, because what matters is the shape rather than the height - as long as you state that the axis does not start at zero.

2. Choosing a flattering time window

library(ggplot2)

full <- data.frame(
  month = 1:12,
  revenue = c(200, 190, 185, 170, 160, 150, 155, 165, 180, 195, 205, 215)
)

ggplot(subset(full, month >= 6), aes(x = month, y = revenue)) +
  geom_line(color = "#16a34a", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Steady growth (looking only from month 6)", x = "Month", y = "Millions")

The second half looks like healthy growth. Now the full year:

library(ggplot2)

full <- data.frame(
  month = 1:12,
  revenue = c(200, 190, 185, 170, 160, 150, 155, 165, 180, 195, 205, 215)
)

ggplot(full, aes(x = month, y = revenue)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2563eb", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 6, xmax = 12, ymin = 145, ymax = 220, alpha = 0.12, fill = "#16a34a") +
  labs(title = "Full year: down through the first half, recovering in the second",
       x = "Month", y = "Millions")

Across the year it is nearly flat - the rise is a recovery from the fall. No number is wrong; only the starting point was chosen.

3. Raw counts instead of rates

library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(
  channel = c("Online", "Store"),
  returns = c(18, 20),
  orders = c(60, 40)
)

ggplot(d, aes(x = channel, y = returns)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  labs(title = "Roughly the same number of returns (?)", x = NULL, y = "Returned orders")

18 against 20, near enough the same. But the two channels handled very different volumes:

library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(
  channel = c("Online", "Store"),
  returns = c(18, 20),
  orders = c(60, 40)
)
d$rate <- round(d$returns / d$orders * 100)

ggplot(d, aes(x = channel, y = rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#dc2626") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(rate, "%")), vjust = -0.4, size = 5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(title = "By rate: the store is far worse", x = NULL, y = "% of orders returned")

30% and 50%. Same data, opposite conclusion. This is the most common of the three - and usually unintentional.

4. Pie charts and what the eye cannot measure

Three more ways to mislead work not on the numbers but on what human eyes are bad at measuring.

The eye compares length very well and angle very badly. Five slices of similar size are all but impossible to rank - while the same data drawn as bars gives up its order immediately:

library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(
  group = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  share = c(23, 21, 19, 19, 18)
)

ggplot(d, aes(x = "", y = share, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  labs(title = "Five near-equal slices - try ranking them by eye", x = NULL, y = NULL)

Now the same data as ordered bars:

library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(
  group = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  share = c(23, 21, 19, 19, 18)
)

ggplot(d, aes(x = reorder(group, -share), y = share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  geom_text(aes(label = share), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(title = "Same data, the order is immediate", x = NULL, y = "Percent")

Two traps of the same family, both about fooling the eye rather than altering the numbers:

  • Area and volume. Double a value and draw it as a circle of double the radius, and the area becomes four times larger. Readers judge by area, so they perceive twice the change that actually happened.
  • Two y-axes on one chart. Putting two differently-scaled quantities on two axes means you choose each scale yourself - and a careful choice makes the lines "move together" or "cross" at will. Two stacked charts sharing one x-axis is the honest version.

5. Checking your own chart

Before sending a chart out, ask five questions:

  1. Does the y axis start at zero? If not, is that stated, and is there a reason?
  2. Is the time window the natural one, or the one that makes the numbers look best?
  3. Are you plotting counts or rates - and are the groups the same size?
  4. Is the reader comparing by length, or being asked to judge angles and areas?
  5. Does the title claim only what the data supports?

Function reference

+---------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------+
|                Function               |                                  What it does                                  |              Example             |
+---------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------+
| coord_cartesian(ylim =)               | Zooms the view without discarding data - the honest way to crop an axis        | coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) |
| ylim() / scale_y_continuous(limits =) | Also sets a range, but removes points outside it, changing computed statistics | ylim(90, 100)                    |
| expand_limits(y = 0)                  | Forces the axis to include zero - the surest way to keep bars uncut            | expand_limits(y = 0)             |
| geom_col()                            | Bars whose height comes straight from the data                                 | geom_col(fill = "#2563eb")       |
| geom_text(aes(label =))               | Puts the number on the chart so nobody has to estimate                         | geom_text(aes(label = share))    |
| reorder(x, -y)                        | Orders groups by value rather than alphabetically                              | reorder(group, -share)           |
| coord_polar(theta = "y")              | Bends bars into a pie - used here to demonstrate why to avoid it               | coord_polar(theta = "y")         |
| coord_flip()                          | Flips the axes when group labels are long                                      | coord_flip()                     |
+---------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------+

Key takeaways

Bars start at zero. The height of a bar is the message. Trend lines may be zoomed, but say so.

Different-sized groups need rates. Raw counts across groups with different denominators compare the wrong thing from the start.

Most misleading charts are not deliberate. They come from taking a convenient default and never checking. The four questions above catch most of them.

lessons.title: Thinking in whole vectors instead of single elements
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 17: Thinking in whole vectors instead of single elements

theory.contentHtml:
People coming from C or Python tend to write R with loops, and then find R slow. In fact R is slow at loops, not at arithmetic - because most of its functions were built to take an entire vector at once.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The same job, two ways
  2. ifelse instead of if inside a loop
  3. Built-in aggregators people forget
  4. Comparing pairwise
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. The same job, two ways

prices <- c(120, 85, 200, 60, 340)
rate <- 0.1

taxed_loop <- numeric(length(prices))
for (i in seq_along(prices)) {
  taxed_loop[i] <- prices[i] * (1 + rate)
}

taxed_vec <- prices * (1 + rate)

print(taxed_loop)
print(taxed_vec)
cat("identical:", identical(taxed_loop, taxed_vec), "\n")

Output:

[1] 132.0  93.5 220.0  66.0 374.0
[1] 132.0  93.5 220.0  66.0 374.0
identical: TRUE

Same result. The vectorised version is shorter, has fewer places to go wrong (no index to misalign), and the multiplication runs in compiled code rather than one pass at a time through R's interpreter.

2. ifelse instead of if inside a loop

if tests one condition; ifelse tests a whole vector:

scores <- c(91, 64, 78, 55, 88)

grade <- ifelse(scores >= 85, "High", ifelse(scores >= 70, "Mid", "Low"))
print(data.frame(scores, grade))

Output:

  scores grade
1     91  High
2     64   Low
3     78   Mid
4     55   Low
5     88  High

Three nested levels is still readable. Beyond that, cut() is far tidier:

scores <- c(91, 64, 78, 55, 88)

grade <- cut(scores,
             breaks = c(-Inf, 69, 84, Inf),
             labels = c("Low", "Mid", "High"))
print(table(grade))

Output:

grade
 Low  Mid High
   2    1    2

cut() also states the boundaries plainly - no tracing through nested ifelse calls to find where the cut-offs are.

3. Built-in aggregators people forget

revenue <- c(120, 85, 200, 60, 340)

cat("running total:", cumsum(revenue), "\n")
cat("running maximum:", cummax(revenue), "\n")
cat("successive differences:", diff(revenue), "\n")
cat("ranks:", rank(revenue), "\n")
cat("reversed:", rev(revenue), "\n")

Output:

running total: 120 205 405 465 805
running maximum: 120 120 200 200 340
successive differences: -35 115 -140 280
ranks: 3 2 4 1 5
reversed: 340 60 200 85 120

Each of these replaces a loop with a state variable - long and easy to get wrong. When you catch yourself about to write "add it up as I go" or "compare with the previous one", reach for cumsum and diff first.

For tables there are rowSums and colMeans:

m <- matrix(c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60), nrow = 2,
            dimnames = list(c("Q1", "Q2"), c("North", "South", "Central")))
print(m)
cat("row totals:", rowSums(m), "\n")
cat("column means:", colMeans(m), "\n")

Output:

   North South Central
Q1    10    30      50
Q2    20    40      60
row totals: 90 120
column means: 15 35 55

4. Comparing pairwise

max() returns one largest value for the whole vector. To compare position by position, use pmax:

bid <- c(100, 250, 180)
floor_price <- c(150, 200, 200)

cat("max  :", max(bid, floor_price), "\n")
cat("pmax :", pmax(bid, floor_price), "\n")

Output:

max  : 250
pmax : 150 250 200

pmax keeps the vector length and compares each position - exactly the job of "take the higher of the bid and the floor price". Reach for max by mistake and you get a single number that R quietly recycles, with no error at all.

Function reference

+--------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+
|         Function         |                                What it does                               |                   Example                  |
+--------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+
| ifelse(test, yes, no)    | Picks per element across a whole vector, returning one of the same length | ifelse(x >= 85, "High", "Mid")             |
| cut(x, breaks, labels)   | Splits numbers into labelled bands - replaces nested ifelse chains        | cut(x, c(-Inf, 69, 84, Inf), labels = ...) |
| cumsum(x)                | Running total up to each position                                         | cumsum(c(1, 2, 3)) → 1 3 6                 |
| cummax(x)                | Largest value seen up to each position                                    | cummax(c(1, 5, 2)) → 1 5 5                 |
| diff(x)                  | Gaps between consecutive elements; result is one element shorter          | diff(c(10, 14, 9)) → 4 -5                  |
| rank(x)                  | Rank of each element within the vector                                    | rank(c(30, 10, 20)) → 3 1 2                |
| rev(x)                   | Reverses the order                                                        | rev(1:3) → 3 2 1                           |
| rowSums(m) / colMeans(m) | Aggregate a matrix or data frame by row / by column                       | rowSums(m)                                 |
| max(x, y)                | One largest value across everything passed in                             | max(c(1, 9), c(5)) → 9                     |
| pmax(x, y)               | Compares position by position, keeping the vector length                  | pmax(c(1, 9), c(5, 5)) → 5 9               |
+--------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

R is slow at loops, not at arithmetic. Moving to vectorised code is usually the single largest speed-up available, and it shortens the code at the same time.

if for one condition, ifelse for a vector. Give if a vector and R looks only at the first element - in recent R versions that is an outright error, but the wrong logic has already spread by then.

max and pmax are different jobs. One collapses the sequence, the other compares pairwise. Mix them up and nothing errors - only the answer is wrong.

lessons.title: Why code slows down as the data grows
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 18: Why code slows down as the data grows

theory.contentHtml:
There is a class of performance bug that never shows up on small data: fine with 100 rows, an endless wait with 100,000. The cause is almost always growing an object inside a loop.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Growing versus preallocating
  2. Why growing is expensive
  3. Collect once instead of rbind in a loop
  4. The hidden cost of looping over a data frame
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. Growing versus preallocating

grow <- function(n) {
  out <- c()
  for (i in 1:n) out <- c(out, i^2)
  out
}

prealloc <- function(n) {
  out <- numeric(n)
  for (i in 1:n) out[i] <- i^2
  out
}

n <- 20000
t1 <- system.time(grow(n))[["elapsed"]]
t2 <- system.time(prealloc(n))[["elapsed"]]

cat("growing      :", round(t1, 3), "seconds\n")
cat("preallocated :", round(t2, 3), "seconds\n")
cat("roughly", round(t1 / max(t2, 0.001)), "times faster\n")

One run - your numbers will differ, so read the ratio between the lines rather than the absolute values:

growing      : 0.439 seconds
preallocated : 0.009 seconds
roughly 49 times faster

Same result, same number of iterations. The difference is that the first version builds a brand-new vector on every pass.

2. Why growing is expensive

c(out, i) does not "append". It allocates a new vector one element longer, copies the whole of the old contents across, and discards the old one.

Iteration 10,000 copies 10,000 elements. Total work grows with the square of the number of iterations - so twice the data takes four times as long. That is the tell: not slower in proportion, but suddenly much slower.

grow <- function(n) {
  out <- c()
  for (i in 1:n) out <- c(out, i)
  out
}

for (n in c(5000, 10000, 20000)) {
  el <- system.time(grow(n))[["elapsed"]]
  cat("n =", n, "->", round(el, 3), "seconds\n")
}

One run:

n = 5000 -> 0.019 seconds
n = 10000 -> 0.086 seconds
n = 20000 -> 0.342 seconds

Each time n doubles the time goes up more than fourfold - 0.019 → 0.086 → 0.342.

Doubling n more than doubles the time - that is the signature of this bug.

3. Collect once instead of rbind in a loop

Stacking rows with rbind is the same mistake in a form you meet more often. What matters is not the number at one size, but the rate of increase when the size doubles:

loop_rbind <- function(n) {
  acc <- NULL
  for (i in 1:n) acc <- rbind(acc, c(i, i * 10))
  acc
}

gather_once <- function(n) do.call(rbind, lapply(1:n, function(i) c(i, i * 10)))

for (n in c(1000, 2000, 4000)) {
  a <- system.time(loop_rbind(n))[["elapsed"]]
  b <- system.time(gather_once(n))[["elapsed"]]
  cat("n =", n, "| in a loop:", round(a, 3), "| gathered once:", round(b, 3), "\n")
}

One run:

n = 1000 | in a loop: 0.003 | gathered once: 0
n = 2000 | in a loop: 0.007 | gathered once: 0.001
n = 4000 | in a loop: 0.026 | gathered once: 0.003

Watch how many times the left column multiplies each time n doubles, against the right: the left grows about fourfold per doubling, the right about twofold. That is quadratic against linear - milliseconds at a few thousand rows, the difference between seconds and an afternoon at a few hundred thousand.

The standard pattern is: collect into a list, then combine once. lapply plus do.call(rbind, ...) - the two tools from module 1.

4. The hidden cost of looping over a data frame

df <- data.frame(x = 1:50000, y = 50000:1)

t_loop <- system.time({
  s <- 0
  for (i in 1:nrow(df)) s <- s + df$x[i] * df$y[i]
})[["elapsed"]]

t_vec <- system.time(s2 <- sum(df$x * df$y))[["elapsed"]]

cat("loop over rows :", round(t_loop, 3), "seconds\n")
cat("vectorised     :", round(t_vec, 3), "seconds\n")
cat("same result:", isTRUE(all.equal(s, s2)), "\n")

One run:

loop over rows : 0.075 seconds
vectorised     : 0 seconds
same result: TRUE

The second line reads exactly 0 - not because it is instant, but because it is faster than the clock can resolve. Section 3 of the next lesson is about precisely that.

Every df$x[i] is an extraction with type and name checking. Do it 50,000 times and that overhead completely swamps the multiplication.

Function reference

+---------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
|          Function         |                                What it does                               |            Example            |
+---------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
| numeric(n)                | Preallocates a numeric vector of n elements, filled with 0                | out <- numeric(1000)          |
| character(n) / logical(n) | Preallocates a character / logical vector                                 | character(50)                 |
| vector("list", n)         | Preallocates a list of n slots - for when each iteration yields an object | res <- vector("list", 100)    |
| seq_along(x)              | Index sequence 1..length(x), safe when x is empty (unlike 1:length(x))    | for (i in seq_along(x))       |
| seq_len(n)                | Sequence 1..n, safe when n = 0                                            | seq_len(nrow(df))             |
| do.call(f, args)          | Calls f with a list of arguments - the gather-once pattern                | do.call(rbind, ds)            |
| system.time(expr)         | Times an expression; take [["elapsed"]]                                   | system.time(f())[["elapsed"]] |
+---------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+

Key takeaways

If you know the size, allocate up front. numeric(n), vector("list", n), character(n) - one line for an order-of-magnitude difference.

If you do not know it, collect into a list and combine once. lapply plus do.call(rbind, ...) instead of rbind inside a loop.

The signature is a sudden jump, not a steady climb. Twice the data taking four times as long means something is growing.

lessons.title: Measure before optimising
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 19: Measure before optimising

theory.contentHtml:
Intuition about where code is slow is almost always wrong. This lesson is about measuring - and about measuring in a way that gives trustworthy numbers, because sloppy timing produces the opposite conclusion.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Timing a piece of code
  2. Repeat to drown out the noise
  3. When the measurement hits the clock floor
  4. Faster is not always worth it
  5. Measuring what you meant to measure
  6. Function reference
  7. Key takeaways

1. Timing a piece of code

x <- runif(200000)

t <- system.time({
  s <- sum(sqrt(x))
})

cat("elapsed:", round(t[["elapsed"]], 4), "seconds\n")
cat("result:", round(s, 1), "\n")

One run (your timing will differ):

elapsed: 0.004 seconds
result: 133392.1

elapsed is wall-clock time - the number a user actually feels. That is the one to report.

2. Repeat to drown out the noise

A single measurement of a fast operation is close to meaningless: the machine is doing other things, and the timer has finite resolution.

bench <- function(expr, times = 30) {
  ts <- numeric(times)
  for (i in seq_len(times)) ts[i] <- system.time(expr())[["elapsed"]]
  c(median = median(ts), fastest = min(ts))
}

x <- runif(50000)

r1 <- bench(function() sum(x^2))
r2 <- bench(function() sum(x * x))

cat("x^2  median:", round(r1[["median"]], 5), "\n")
cat("x*x  median:", round(r2[["median"]], 5), "\n")

One run:

x^2  median: 0.001
x*x  median: 0

Those two numbers do not answer the question yet - which is what the next section is about.

Use the median, not the mean - one moment of the machine being busy drags a mean badly, while the median shrugs it off.

3. When the measurement hits the clock floor

Look again at what just came back: one side 0.001 seconds, the other exactly 0. It is not that x * x is instant - it is faster than the clock can see. system.time has a finite resolution, and anything quicker than one tick is recorded as zero.

Repeating 30 times does not rescue it, because each repetition is still its own measurement and each one still hits the floor. The median of a list of zeros is zero.

The fix: put the loop inside the measurement, then divide by the number of runs.

x <- runif(50000)

t_once <- system.time(sum(x * x))[["elapsed"]]
t_many <- system.time(for (i in 1:200) sum(x * x))[["elapsed"]] / 200

cat("timed once  :", t_once, "seconds\n")
cat("timed 200x  :", round(t_many, 7), "seconds each\n")

One run:

timed once  : 0.001 seconds
timed 200x  : 0.000555 seconds each

The single measurement lands on zero or jumps a whole tick. The repeated one lands below a tick - a number the old approach could never see.

Now there is a number to compare. The rule: if a measurement comes back as 0, do not conclude "infinitely fast" - make the work big enough for the clock to see it.

For the same reason, never take a ratio between two measurements when the denominator is zero. "Infinitely faster" only ever means you have not measured anything.

4. Faster is not always worth it

x <- runif(100000)

t_sapply <- system.time(a <- sapply(x, function(v) v * 2))[["elapsed"]]
t_vec <- system.time(b <- x * 2)[["elapsed"]]

cat("sapply     :", round(t_sapply, 4), "seconds\n")
cat("vectorised :", round(t_vec, 4), "seconds\n")
cat("same result:", isTRUE(all.equal(a, b)), "\n")

One run:

sapply     : 0.046 seconds
vectorised : 0 seconds
same result: TRUE

That zero again, from section 3 - the vectorised version is faster than the clock floor, so this is enough to say "much faster" but not enough to say how many times faster.

The gap here is large and worth taking, because the vectorised version is also shorter. But an optimisation that saves 20 milliseconds in a script that runs once a night, at the cost of harder-to-read code, is a net loss.

The right order is: make it correct, then measure, then optimise only what measurement shows is genuinely slow.

5. Measuring what you meant to measure

R evaluates lazily, so a measurement can slide off the thing you had in mind:

slow_sum <- function(n) {
  s <- 0
  for (i in 1:n) s <- s + i
  s
}

t_wrong <- system.time(f <- function() slow_sum(200000))[["elapsed"]]
t_right <- system.time(slow_sum(200000))[["elapsed"]]

cat("only DEFINING a function:", round(t_wrong, 4), "seconds\n")
cat("actually RUNNING it     :", round(t_right, 4), "seconds\n")

One run:

only DEFINING a function: 0 seconds
actually RUNNING it     : 0.02 seconds

The first measurement is near zero because it only defines a function and never runs it. This is the easiest way to convince yourself you have just optimised something.

Same class of mistake: timing the first call of a library that has not loaded yet, or timing on data thousands of times smaller than the real thing.

Function reference

+--------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
|      Function      |                                     What it does                                     |            Example            |
+--------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+
| system.time(expr)  | Times an expression                                                                  | system.time(f(x))             |
| [["elapsed"]]      | Takes the wall-clock time - the number a user actually feels                         | system.time(f())[["elapsed"]] |
| median(x)          | Median - survives one busy moment on the machine, unlike mean                        | median(ts)                    |
| min(x)             | Best run seen, a lower bound on the true cost                                        | min(ts)                       |
| runif(n)           | Draws n uniform random numbers - building data to measure against                    | x <- runif(2e5)               |
| replicate(n, expr) | Runs an expression n times and collects the results                                  | replicate(30, f())            |
| all.equal(a, b)    | Checks two results are approximately equal - proving the fast version is still right | isTRUE(all.equal(a, b))       |
+--------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------+

Key takeaways

Measure first, change second. Where you assume the time goes and where it actually goes rarely coincide.

Repeat and take the median. A single measurement records the state of the machine as much as the code.

Check that you are really running what you think. Timing an expression that was never evaluated is the commonest way to produce a beautiful, meaningless number.

A measurement of 0 means you have not measured yet, not that it is infinitely fast. Put the loop inside the measurement and divide - and never take a ratio with zero in the denominator.

questions.prompt: out <- c(); for (i in 1:n) out <- c(out, i) - why is this dreadfully slow for large n?

options.label: A
options.text: Because each c() allocates a new vector and copies all the old contents

options.label: B
options.text: Because R's for is always slow whatever it does

options.label: C
options.text: Because 1:n uses a lot of memory

options.label: D
options.text: Because set.seed is missing

questions.explanation: Total work grows with the square of the iteration count - twice the data takes four times as long. Preallocating with numeric(n) removes the copying entirely.

questions.prompt: You do not know the number of result rows in advance. What is the right pattern for combining many data frames?

options.label: A
options.text: rbind each row onto an accumulator inside the loop

options.label: B
options.text: Write to a file and read it back

options.label: C
options.text: Collect into a list and combine once: do.call(rbind, lapply(...))

options.label: D
options.text: Use merge instead of rbind

questions.explanation: rbind inside a loop is the heavier form of the growing bug. Collecting first and combining once copies exactly once.

questions.prompt: bid <- c(100, 250, 180), floor <- c(150, 200, 200). To take the higher value at each position, use what?

options.label: A
options.text: max(bid, floor)

options.label: B
options.text: sort(c(bid, floor))

options.label: C
options.text: cummax(bid)

options.label: D
options.text: pmax(bid, floor)

questions.explanation: max collapses everything to a single number which R then quietly recycles. Nothing errors - only the answer is wrong.

questions.prompt: You time something that takes a few milliseconds with a single system.time call. What is the problem?

options.label: A
options.text: system.time cannot measure under a second

options.label: B
options.text: One measurement records the state of the machine too - repeat and take the median

options.label: C
options.text: You must use Sys.time() for accuracy

options.label: D
options.text: There is no problem

questions.explanation: Median rather than mean: one moment of the machine being busy drags a mean badly, while the median ignores it.

questions.prompt: system.time(f <- function() slow_sum(200000)) reports close to 0 seconds. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: Because slow_sum really is that fast

options.label: B
options.text: Because R cached the result

options.label: C
options.text: Because that line only defines a function and never runs it

options.label: D
options.text: Because system.time skips functions

questions.explanation: This is the easiest way to convince yourself you just optimised something: timing an expression that was never evaluated gives a beautiful, meaningless number.

questions.prompt: An optimisation saves 20 milliseconds in a script that runs once a night, in exchange for considerably harder-to-read code. Worth it?

options.label: A
options.text: No - the reading cost far outweighs 20ms a night

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, faster is always better

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, to prepare for larger data later

options.label: D
options.text: It depends on the programming language

questions.explanation: Correct first, measure second, optimise only what measurement shows is genuinely slow. Micro-optimisation paid for in readability is nearly always a loss.

questions.prompt: Timing sum(x * x) with system.time returns exactly 0 seconds, and the median over 30 repeats is still 0. What does that mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The work is faster than the clock can resolve - nothing has been measured yet; run it many times inside a single measurement and divide

options.label: B
options.text: The operation is instant and needs no further optimisation

options.label: C
options.text: system.time is broken and a different timing library is needed

options.label: D
options.text: Taking the median is wrong; the mean would give a non-zero number

questions.explanation: Repeating 30 times does not help, because each repetition is its own measurement and each one still hits the floor - the median of a list of zeros is zero. Put the loop inside system.time and divide by the number of runs. For the same reason, never take a ratio between two timings when the denominator is zero.

lessons.title: Stopping bad data at the door
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 21: Stopping bad data at the door

theory.contentHtml:
When a function receives something it did not expect, there are two outcomes. The good one is an immediate error. The bad one is a perfectly ordinary-looking number - and that number goes straight into the report.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. When a function quietly returns the wrong answer
  2. Checking at the top of the function
  3. Error messages written for whoever must fix it
  4. Warnings when you can still continue
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. When a function quietly returns the wrong answer

avg_price <- function(prices, qty) sum(prices * qty) / sum(qty)

cat("correct:", avg_price(c(10, 20), c(3, 7)), "\n")
cat("mismatched lengths:", avg_price(c(10, 20, 30, 40), c(3, 7)), "\n")

Output:

correct: 17
mismatched lengths: 54

The second call passes vectors of mismatched length: 4 and 2. R silently repeats the shorter one to fill and returns a number - no error, not a single warning. If this were the average selling price in a quarterly report, nobody would catch it.

Worth noting: R only warns when the lengths are not multiples of each other (3 and 2, say). In the most dangerous case - when one length divides the other - it stays completely silent.

That is why you check at the door, not because it is tidier.

2. Checking at the top of the function

stopifnot() is the shortest way:

avg_price <- function(prices, qty) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(prices), is.numeric(qty), length(prices) == length(qty))
  sum(prices * qty) / sum(qty)
}

cat(avg_price(c(10, 20), c(3, 7)), "\n")

res <- try(avg_price(c(10, 20, 30), c(3, 7)), silent = TRUE)
cat("error caught:", inherits(res, "try-error"), "\n")

Output:

17
error caught: TRUE

Now bad data stops right where it entered, instead of spreading downstream and failing somewhere unrelated.

3. Error messages written for whoever must fix it

stopifnot prints the violated expression - fine for you, a bit curt for anyone else. stop() lets you write a sentence:

avg_price <- function(prices, qty) {
  if (length(prices) != length(qty)) {
    stop("prices and qty must be the same length (got ", length(prices),
         " and ", length(qty), ")")
  }
  if (sum(qty) == 0) stop("total quantity is 0, cannot compute an average price")
  sum(prices * qty) / sum(qty)
}

res <- try(avg_price(c(10, 20, 30), c(3, 7)), silent = TRUE)
cat(conditionMessage(attr(res, "condition")), "\n")

Output:

prices and qty must be the same length (got 3 and 2)

A good message says three things: what is wrong, what the actual values are, and implicitly where to fix it. Compare that with Error in prices * qty : non-conformable arrays.

Note the sum(qty) == 0 guard too - dividing by zero does not raise an error in R, it returns NaN or Inf and drifts onward.

4. Warnings when you can still continue

Not every irregularity deserves to stop the whole program:

avg_price <- function(prices, qty) {
  stopifnot(length(prices) == length(qty))
  keep <- !is.na(prices) & !is.na(qty)
  if (any(!keep)) warning("skipped ", sum(!keep), " rows containing NA")
  sum(prices[keep] * qty[keep]) / sum(qty[keep])
}

r <- withCallingHandlers(
  avg_price(c(10, NA, 30), c(3, 7, 2)),
  warning = function(w) {
    cat("warning:", conditionMessage(w), "\n")
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
cat("result:", round(r, 2), "\n")

Output:

warning: skipped 1 rows containing NA
result: 18

The line to draw: stop when you cannot produce a correct result; warning when you can but the caller needs to know something was dropped. Silently discarding the NA rows is the worst of the three options.

Function reference

+---------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------+
|             Function            |                               What it does                               |                  Example                 |
+---------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------+
| stopifnot(...)                  | Halts as soon as a condition is false, printing the offending expression | stopifnot(length(a) == length(b))        |
| stop(...)                       | Halts with a message you write - actual values can be pasted in          | stop("got ", n, " rows")                 |
| warning(...)                    | Reports something odd but carries on                                     | warning("skipped ", k, " rows")          |
| is.numeric(x) / is.character(x) | Type checks at the door                                                  | is.numeric(prices)                       |
| length(x)                       | Vector length - the mismatch R silently recycles                         | length(a) == length(b)                   |
| is.na(x)                        | Logical vector marking the missing cells                                 | keep <- !is.na(x)                        |
| any(x) / all(x)                 | At least one / every element is TRUE                                     | if (any(!keep)) ...                      |
| try(expr, silent = TRUE)        | Runs and swallows the error, returning a try-error object to inspect     | inherits(res, "try-error")               |
| withCallingHandlers(...)        | Catches a warning without unwinding the rest of the call                 | pair with invokeRestart("muffleWarning") |
+---------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

The dangerous case is not an error, it is a wrong answer that looks right. Vector recycling, division by zero, silently dropped NAs - all produce numbers that go straight into a report.

Check at the top of the function. A fault caught where the data arrives is far easier to fix than one that surfaces three calls later.

Error messages should include the actual values. "must be the same length (got 3 and 2)" lets someone fix it immediately; "invalid argument" does not.

lessons.title: Catching errors without swallowing them
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 22: Catching errors without swallowing them

theory.contentHtml:
When you run a job across twenty files, one bad file should not kill the batch. But "catch it and carry on" slides very easily into "hide it" - which is how wrong numbers appear with nobody able to trace where they came from.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. tryCatch: catch and handle
  2. Carrying on past a broken item
  3. Cleaning up whether it worked or not
  4. Why swallowing errors is dangerous
  5. Function reference
  6. Key takeaways

1. tryCatch: catch and handle

parse_amount <- function(x) {
  tryCatch(
    as.numeric(x) * 1000,
    warning = function(w) NA_real_,
    error = function(e) NA_real_
  )
}

cat(parse_amount("12"), "\n")
cat(parse_amount("twelve"), "\n")

Output:

12000
NA

tryCatch takes the main expression, then handlers by kind of condition. Returning NA is reasonable here because the function only converts - but those NAs must be counted at the level above.

2. Carrying on past a broken item

sources <- list(c(1, 2, 3), "broken", c(10, 20))

results <- lapply(seq_along(sources), function(i) {
  tryCatch(
    list(ok = TRUE, value = sum(sources[[i]])),
    error = function(e) list(ok = FALSE, value = NA, why = conditionMessage(e))
  )
})

for (i in seq_along(results)) {
  r <- results[[i]]
  if (r$ok) cat("source", i, ": total =", r$value, "\n")
  else cat("source", i, ": FAILED -", r$why, "\n")
}

cat("summary:", sum(sapply(results, function(r) r$ok)), "/", length(results), "succeeded\n")

Output:

source 1 : total = 6
source 2 : FAILED - invalid 'type' (character) of argument
source 3 : total = 30
summary: 2 / 3 succeeded

The pattern that matters here: each result carries both its status and the reason. That is what lets the final line say "2 of 3 succeeded" instead of quietly handing back two numbers as though all was well.

3. Cleaning up whether it worked or not

finally always runs - use it to close connections, delete temporary files, restore options:

old <- options(digits = 7)

run_with_precision <- function(x) {
  tryCatch({
    options(digits = 3)
    if (x < 0) stop("negative input not accepted")
    sqrt(x)
  },
  error = function(e) NA_real_,
  finally = options(old))
}

cat(run_with_precision(2), "\n")
cat(run_with_precision(-1), "\n")
cat("digits restored:", getOption("digits"), "\n")

Output:

1.414214
NA
digits restored: 7

Without finally, the error path would leave digits = 3 for the rest of the session - a side effect that is very hard to track down.

4. Why swallowing errors is dangerous

totals <- c(120, 240, 310)

# Catching, but recording nothing
quiet <- sapply(totals, function(t) tryCatch(t / 0, error = function(e) NA))
cat("silent:", quiet, "\n")

# Checking, and saying so
loud <- sapply(totals, function(t) {
  if (!is.finite(t / 0)) {
    cat("warning: division by zero at value", t, "\n")
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  t / 0
})
cat("reported:", loud, "\n")

Output:

silent: Inf Inf Inf
warning: division by zero at value 120
warning: division by zero at value 240
warning: division by zero at value 310
reported: NA NA NA

Division by zero in R does not throw - so the tryCatch above catches nothing and Inf sails straight through. Catching errors is no substitute for checking conditions.

The rule: a tryCatch whose handler records nothing is almost always wrong. Count at the very least; better, keep the reason.

Function reference

+-------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
|                  Function                 |                              What it does                              |                 Example                |
+-------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| tryCatch(expr, error = f)                 | Runs expr; on error calls f instead of halting                         | tryCatch(f(x), error = function(e) NA) |
| tryCatch(..., warning = f)                | Catches warnings on their own branch, separate from errors             | warning = function(w) NA               |
| tryCatch(..., finally = expr)             | Runs expr whether it succeeded or failed - where cleanup goes          | finally = options(old)                 |
| conditionMessage(e)                       | Pulls the text out of an error or warning, for logging                 | conditionMessage(e)                    |
| on.exit(expr)                             | Registers cleanup at the top of a function, run when it returns        | on.exit(options(old))                  |
| options(digits = n) / getOption("digits") | Reads and sets global options - the kind that must be restored         | old <- options(digits = 2)             |
| suppressWarnings(expr)                    | Silences warnings - for when you know exactly why, not for convenience | suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))        |
| inherits(x, "try-error")                  | Checks whether a result is a swallowed error                           | inherits(res, "try-error")             |
+-------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+

Key takeaways

Results should carry their status. list(ok =, value =, why =) lets the level above report honestly instead of assuming everything ran.

finally is for cleanup. Every global option change, connection and temporary file gets restored there.

Swallowing an error is not handling it. An error handler that returns NA without counting or logging is exactly how wrong numbers reach a report untraceably.

lessons.title: Testing your own functions
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 23: Testing your own functions

theory.contentHtml:
You do not need a testing library to start testing. A few lines of plain R catch most regressions - and more importantly, they force you to write down what you believe is true.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The smallest possible test
  2. Comparing floating-point numbers properly
  3. Testing the cases that must fail
  4. Edge cases are where the bugs live
  5. A suite that is always green has not been tested
  6. Function reference
  7. Key takeaways

1. The smallest possible test

avg_price <- function(prices, qty) {
  stopifnot(length(prices) == length(qty), sum(qty) > 0)
  sum(prices * qty) / sum(qty)
}

check <- function(label, actual, expected) {
  ok <- isTRUE(all.equal(actual, expected))
  cat(if (ok) "PASS" else "FAIL", label, "\n")
  ok
}

results <- c(
  check("single element", avg_price(10, 5), 10),
  check("equal weights", avg_price(c(10, 20), c(1, 1)), 15),
  check("uneven weights", avg_price(c(10, 20), c(3, 1)), 12.5)
)

cat(sum(results), "/", length(results), "checks passed\n")

Output:

PASS single element
PASS equal weights
PASS uneven weights
3 / 3 checks passed

Those three lines are already enough to tell you whether your next edit breaks something. That is the whole value of testing.

2. Comparing floating-point numbers properly

cat("0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3        :", 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, "\n")
cat("all.equal(0.1+0.2, 0.3) :", isTRUE(all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)), "\n")

Output:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3        : FALSE
all.equal(0.1+0.2, 0.3) : TRUE

Floating-point numbers are binary approximations, so == returns FALSE on an obviously correct sum. Always use all.equal for real numbers, wrapped in isTRUE - because when they differ, all.equal returns a description string rather than FALSE.

3. Testing the cases that must fail

A function must raise an error on bad input - and that deserves a test of its own:

avg_price <- function(prices, qty) {
  stopifnot(length(prices) == length(qty), sum(qty) > 0)
  sum(prices * qty) / sum(qty)
}

expect_error <- function(label, expr) {
  failed <- inherits(try(expr, silent = TRUE), "try-error")
  cat(if (failed) "PASS" else "FAIL", label, "\n")
}

expect_error("mismatched lengths must fail", avg_price(c(1, 2, 3), c(1, 2)))
expect_error("zero total quantity must fail", avg_price(c(1, 2), c(0, 0)))

Output:

PASS mismatched lengths must fail
PASS zero total quantity must fail

Without this, one day someone deletes the stopifnot line to "tidy up", and the function quietly goes back to returning wrong numbers.

4. Edge cases are where the bugs live

Every function passes the ordinary case. Bugs live at the edges:

count_positive <- function(x) sum(x > 0, na.rm = TRUE)

cases <- list(
  list("empty vector", numeric(0), 0),
  list("all negative", c(-1, -5), 0),
  list("contains NA", c(1, NA, 3), 2),
  list("contains zero", c(0, 1, 2), 2)
)

for (cs in cases) {
  got <- count_positive(cs[[2]])
  cat(if (isTRUE(all.equal(got, cs[[3]]))) "PASS" else "FAIL",
      cs[[1]], "- got", got, "\n")
}

Output:

PASS empty vector - got 0
PASS all negative - got 0
PASS contains NA - got 2
PASS contains zero - got 2

The edge-case list to run through every time: empty, one element, contains NA, contains zero, all values identical, negative values, and ties wherever there is sorting or ranking.

5. A suite that is always green has not been tested

All four sections above end in a row of PASS. But a row of PASS does not prove what you think it does: it can mean the function is right, or it can mean the tests are incapable of failing.

The way to tell them apart: break the function on purpose and see whether the suite goes red.

count_positive <- function(x) sum(x > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
broken <- function(x) sum(x >= 0, na.rm = TRUE)   # wrong when a zero is present

run_suite <- function(f) {
  cases <- list(list(numeric(0), 0), list(c(-1, -5), 0),
                list(c(1, NA, 3), 2), list(c(0, 1, 2), 2))
  sum(vapply(cases, function(cs) isTRUE(all.equal(f(cs[[1]]), cs[[2]])), logical(1)))
}

cat("correct version:", run_suite(count_positive), "/ 4 passed\n")
cat("broken version :", run_suite(broken), "/ 4 passed\n")

Output:

correct version: 4 / 4 passed
broken version : 3 / 4 passed

The broken version fails exactly one case - the "contains zero" one. Had it passed all four, the suite would be the thing needing repair, not the function.

The broken version has to fail at least one case. If it sails through, the suite is not touching the behaviour you meant to protect - and it will stay green right up until somebody really does change the function.

This is also why a suite made only of ordinary cases is close to worthless: the broken version passes those too.

Function reference

+--------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------+
|         Function         |                                What it does                               |           Example          |
+--------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------+
| all.equal(a, b)          | Approximate comparison - the right way to compare doubles                 | all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)  |
| isTRUE(x)                | Forces a plain TRUE/FALSE - required around all.equal                     | isTRUE(all.equal(a, b))    |
| identical(a, b)          | Exact comparison including type - for integers, strings, structures       | identical(x, y)            |
| try(expr, silent = TRUE) | Runs and swallows the error, so the must-fail branch can be tested        | try(f(bad), silent = TRUE) |
| inherits(x, "try-error") | True when try has just caught an error                                    | inherits(res, "try-error") |
| vapply(x, f, FUN.VALUE)  | Like sapply but pins the return type - tests cannot silently change shape | vapply(cs, f, logical(1))  |
| numeric(0)               | The empty vector - an edge case worth asking about every time             | f(numeric(0))              |
| na.rm = TRUE             | Drops missing values when aggregating; without it the answer is NA        | sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)       |
+--------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------------------+

Key takeaways

A test that calls a function without asserting anything is useless. It stays green even when the function returns rubbish.

all.equal for real numbers, == for integers and strings. And remember isTRUE - all.equal returns a description string when values differ, and a string inside if is an error.

Test the must-fail branch too. Otherwise your input guards can be removed with nothing objecting.
